#6061. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6060. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

Given the dire state of the BA offer with still flaky IT, dirty badly maintained cabins and dysfunctional (if at all) customer services a great option for those in the UK.

#6057. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6056. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6055. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6054. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6053. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6052. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6051. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6049. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

Looking for a new airplane model? Head over to our friends at the Midwest Model Store for a wide selection of airlines and liveries.

#6048. Review: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres (Hyatt Inclusive)

Of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection. My stay was almost exactly 24 hours and solo which is uncharacteristic at this destination resort. My experience will likely differ from other guests due to those factors.

Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026. It sits on a stretch of white-sand beach in Costa Mujeres, 12 miles north of Cancun. Cancun International Airport is the arrival airport. I could not confirm a single official transfer time from the property page. Tour listings commonly put the drive in a 30 to 45 minute range.

Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico

Google Maps: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres

Hyatt is the best in the business at high end resort arrivals. I had given my name at the security gate and by the time I reached the lobby, the door to the vehicle was opened for me, I was greeted by name and a “welcome home”, a constant refrain throughout my stay. It’s a small thing and maybe cliché but it was effective. I was given a Globalist upgrade even though rules at all-inclusives differ from the rest of the chain. As my upgrade was in a Preferred room, I was brought into a private room at the front of the lobby where check-in was done for me.

The lobby is an open-air room under an arched woven ceiling, with a direct view out to the ocean.

The resort is spread across 10 buildings with 505 keys. Of those, 221 are Preferred Club keys with an elevated experience. My building (and others like it) had just five rooms on each floor and just five floors which made it feel boutique rather than massive. Every oceanfront room is Preferred Club, and so are the first two buildings on either side.

The room views follow a simple rule by floor. Every first floor room is a swim-out, floors two through four are tropical view, and the fifth floor is ocean view or ocean front. That makes booking easy to reason through: if you want to step off your patio into the water, go low, and if you want the sea, go high.

The walkways give a sense of grandeur and space. All of the flora is local, and in a touch I loved, the service rooms are named after the plants.

There are four pools, and each one has a unique characteristic. The Jungle pool is drinks only and hidden in the middle of the resort by trees. The Social pool runs activities throughout the day at this adults-only resort for those who want to participate. There is also an infinity pool on the edge of the beach, and then the Preferred Club pool for those staying in that category. These are separate from the first floor swim-outs.

The spa (hydrotherapy is included for Preferred guests) featured an outdoor circuit that included both hot and cold plunge pools, amongst other therapeutic services.

The Preferred Club pool was the most frequented, though some images below look more vacant due to rain that rolled through during my opportunity to collect media on my short stay.

The gym is open to every guest from 6 AM to 8 PM, and it is outfitted with Technogym equipment.

The spa is open 8 AM to 8 PM with 17 treatment cabins and a beauty salon, and hydrotherapy is included. That last part is the headline. The hydrotherapy space is ridiculous, easily the standout of the entire property for me, and it is the kind of amenity that would make me pick this resort over a competitor down the beach. There are indoor and outdoor showers as well.

The men’s changing room featured private showers with an option for indoor or outdoor experiences.

The theater seats 264 people and hosts cabaret and Mayan shows. There are also pickleball courts, which I am starting to think should be required equipment at any resort that wants a younger crowd as well as padel for the European set (and growing American interest.)

Secrets is an adults-only brand, and every room here comes with what the company calls Unlimited-Luxury. For a standard guest that means unlimited dining and top-shelf drinks, Wi-Fi, daytime activities and nightly entertainment, with tips and taxes included. Add 24-hour room service, a mini-bar refreshed daily (you can ask for just about anything you want in there), and pool and beach wait service for all guests.

The Preferred Club is an upgrade, and at this resort it is a big one because it owns the oceanfront. Secrets lists personalized check-in and check-out, afternoon hot and cold hors d’oeuvres, desserts and premium liquors, access to the Preferred Club lounge and beach bar, an upgraded mini-bar, upgraded bath amenities, butler service, Bali beds at the pool and beach reserved for club guests, and exclusive dining at the Preferred Club beach restaurant. Preferred also gives club guests exclusive access to an infinity pool and puts an oversized soaking tub on the terrace of the upgraded suites (at least with the oceanfronts).

I book a lot of Hyatt’s all-inclusives through Hyatt Privé rates, and this resort is one of 388 in the collection. Privé is Hyatt’s invitation-only program for travel advisors, so you only get the benefits when an approved advisor makes the booking, and the stay still earns World of Hyatt points and elite nights.

The all-inclusive version of Privé looks a lot different from a Park Hyatt booking. As I wrote when Hyatt’s all-inclusive resorts joined Privé, there is no room upgrade and no breakfast benefit, since every meal is already included. At this property, Privé guests receive a $100 resort credit per stay, a welcome amenity and letter, hydrotherapy access, and early check-in and late check-out based on availability.

Elite status matters here more than at most all-inclusives. Under World of Hyatt’s terms, Globalists get the best room available at check-in, including rooms with club access, at the resort’s discretion. Explorists are eligible for upgrades too, but not to standard suites or club rooms. Travelers who have stayed at Secrets resorts as Globalists report being designated Preferred Club guests even when they did not land in a club building, which unlocks the lounge, pool and beach areas. This was my experience on all accounts at the resort. Late checkout is 2 PM for Explorists and 4 PM for Globalists, subject to availability at resorts. It was able to honor my request for a late check-out, I did not arrive early enough to request the early check-in. Hyatt waives resort fees on eligible paid rates (at least for now) and award nights for Globalists, and on award nights only for every other tier, and Globalists also get free parking on free nights though in 2028 Globalists will have to select this as a preference. One catch is that Suite Upgrade Awards cannot be used at Secrets resorts, so you cannot lock in a suite with one here.

Weddings are big business here. The courtyard outside the theater is the setting, with the sunset behind it, and the resort hosts lots of them. The resort disclosed its occupancy to me but it wasn’t clear if it was for public consumption. It was shockingly high especially for a Thursday in mid-November. Over the holidays or spring break all the hotels are full but this is a period where I would have expected a lull. Still, despite being extremely full, it never felt crowded.

For meetings and groups, the convention space measures 9,800 square feet and splits into five sections. The boardroom was occupied at the time so I couldn’t include images of that.

Restaurants can be booked in advance through the Hyatt Inclusive Collection app, which I wish more all-inclusives offered. Nobody wants to find out at 7 PM that the restaurant they wanted is full and through the app this can be done well in advance of a guest’s arrival. The dress code in the restaurants is resort casual, though the patio does not require slacks and closed toed shoes for men, shorts are acceptable outside.

The restaurants include: Portofino (Italian), Bordeaux (French), Himitsu (pan-Asian, with sushi and teppanyaki), Oceana (seafood in an open-air setting), Barefoot Grill (light lunch), Market Café (the international buffet, which I noted on site as the Marketplace), Seaside Grill (a poolside grill), and Coco Café. The bars on that list include Rendezvous in the lobby, Barracuda on the beach, a swim-up bar, a beach bar, and the Preferred Club beach bar and lounge bar. There’s also a Sports Bar and Lounge next to the theater.

Oceana is the seafood restaurant, set in an open-air dining room with woven pendant lamps, macrame hangings and a pebble mosaic floor. I chose this for my one dinner on property during my brief stay.

I started with the lamb croquettes, which the menu serves with yogurt and sweet chili sauce, cashews, watercress and a pickled shallot salad, and the Iberian salad with fresh mozzarella, prosciutto, rucula, toasted pistachios, balsamic and roasted peach. A crusty loaf came with the meal.

For a main I had the coconut shrimp, served with parsley orzo pasta, coconut sauce and parmesan crispy, and finished with the mango cheesecake, which the menu plates with vanilla cream and a mango compote with honey and basil.

Market Café, the international buffet I noted as the Marketplace, serves breakfast until 11:30 AM. [TO CONFIRM: lunch and dinner service at Market Café]

Seaside Grill hosts the Preferred Club à la carte breakfast. The official dining page says breakfast there is served for Preferred Club guests only. I tried a number of dishes for lunch to report to our fine audience.

Rendezvous sits at the heart of the property with 360-degree access, so you can walk up to it from any direction.

Preferred Club guests get their own bar at the beach, and the Preferred Club lounge also has an indoor lounge for when the sun gets to be too much.

My room was a Preferred Oceanfront King, a single open room with a king bed against a macrame headboard wall, rattan pendant lights, a ceiling fan, and a daybed sofa facing a marble bistro table. The balcony with jacuzzi looks straight over the beach. In the bathroom, a freestanding tub sits under a wood-slat ceiling beside a walk-in rain shower with a pebble floor and a bench. The double vanity has vessel sinks, round mirrors and a wave-textured wall, and the shower is stocked with Le Labo Bergamote 22 shampoo, conditioner and shower gel. Le Labo is a confirmed winner for me.

I also had the chance to tour a master suites, all of which are oceanfront, and they are also available as swim-outs.

Every first floor room is a swim-out, opening onto the pool.

Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an incredible resort that somehow felt small when you were in your building but big enough to have everything. For my stay, I used 45,000 points on a no-notice booking to offset a $1,300/night stay. I have seen rates from $560 for off-season which is without question worth it. I loved the property and I look forward to returning with more time and my wife, but the adults-only nature of the property will make it a harder stay for us to achieve.

What do you think? Have you stayed at Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres?

#6047. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

#6045. Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

Last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2. It also offered a faster track for Delta Diamond, Delta 360, AA Executive Platinum and Concierge Key members: earn 50 tiles by year-end and get Mosaic 4. That worked out to $5,000 in JetBlue flights or Paisly packages, or $50,000 on the JetBlue card, and a single Mint roundtrip to Europe could cover most of it. I already had AA Executive Platinum, so I didn’t need the status. I wanted it anyway. JetBlue was adding routes from my home airports, I fly to Boston, New York and Fort Lauderdale often, and the United partnership raised the possibility of benefits on both sides.

My application was approved just before the June 30 deadline. Some applicants waited up to six weeks for processing, though, and losing six weeks of a 12-week challenge is a real cost. JetBlue then added its 25-for-25 promotion on top. Visiting 25 destinations by year-end earned up to 350,000 TrueBlue points plus 25 years of Mosaic 1, which made a cheap, aggressive weekend of short hops look worth it. My plan was to finish the challenge through spend and put the points toward transatlantic and Japan trips. My one worry at the time was whether JetBlue would treat these new Mosaics well enough to keep them flying with it.

My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW). I occasionally also fly from Fort Lauderdale or Miami when it makes sense. But Pittsburgh had just flights to Boston for some of last year, before adding Fort Lauderdale to fill the Spirit gap and then New York JFK competing with Delta, and more broadly to the New York market, United and American with more than enough flights. From Fort Myers, it’s Boston of JFK.

I flew once to Boston on JetBlue but at the time, it had not yet launched a domestic first class, a better seat selection included in my fare was the only real enhancement to the short flight of just over 80 minutes. I’ll cover other reasons why I wasn’t able to fly the carrier more, but given that I am not in New York, Boston, or Fort Lauderdale full time, every flight I take has a connection and it’s not particularly on-the-way for me. For example, if heading south to Florida, Charlotte, Atlanta, or even Washington Dulles make more sense than Boston or New York but when heading west at all, Chicago, Houston, Dallas, and Denver are all obviously better options.

Even to Europe, there’s not a material advantage with limited schedules and limited footprint on the continent. For trips to Paris given that I will have to connect anyway, I have more options on any other carrier through east coast hubs than with JetBlue on its metal not to mention partner networks.

Most recently, I had a flight to Cancun and with airport time, flight time and connections, it’s faster to fly out of Miami or Fort Lauderdale. But JetBlue had fewer flights for more money and far more miles than with American. Outside of the northeast corridor or based in South(east) Florida, I couldn’t make it make sense.

I’m heading to Europe for a meeting next week and I will finally have a chance to try Mint. This will constitute two of my longest flights with JetBlue ever. I haven’t heard many negative comments about JetBlue Mint, and I have high expectations. It’s hard to get excited about another American or United flight in business class solely because I have flown those so often and there’s little new there.

I’ll get a chance to try a reasonably long three-hour flight domestically to see how it differs from my prior JetBlue experience. Then, assuming flights are on time, I should have a chance to try the new BlueHouse, a first for me. Following that is a long haul flight in Mint and I am looking forward to the experience.

Statistically, I can’t see a reason that I try for Mosaic again, but who knows? The experience could change what appears to be a clear analytical decision for me at this point.

One of the biggest reasons I secure status via flying/spending/staying is to redeem systemwide upgrades (or suite upgrades in the case of hotels.) I’ll fully admit that upon receiving approval for the challenge last year, I hadn’t even considered that Mint certificates would work differently than other upgrade certificates in the industry. One upgrade certificate is worth an upgrade (if available.) United uses “Plus Points” but it feels clearer that there will be some variability in what’s required to move between the cabins.

For this particular trip, JetBlue wanted two upgrade certificates in one direction, and four on another. Thankfully, I had taken the upgrade option every time I achieved a choice to select a benefit, but had I chosen something else assuming that I’d only need two Move to Mint certificates (as I would with American for example) I would have come up short.

I covered how much spending is required to achieve top tier status and its associated benefits in recent posts. This was in response to United’s move to require $480,000 in annual spending (by credit card only) to achieve United 1K status. Assuming that along the way loyalty points are taken and annual Mosaic bonuses are applied to cardholders, JetBlue is above American at $225,000 in spend for Mosaic 4 vs. American’s net of $164,000 for Executive Platinum with just two systemwide upgrades, or $214,000 with six. The difference is that those six upgrades apply for the full-one-way on a single certificate.

I spent time trying to figure out why one way charged four Move to Mint vs two and in the end, it didn’t really matter. I can nearly upgrade my entire family of four on American vs a single roundtrip for myself. For what it’s worth, the base cost was also more expensive with JetBlue than American for which I had upgrades available.

I have the qualified business spend to earn Mosaic 4 every year, but the value of its perks aren’t even close to the rest of the market. And for what JetBlue expects in spend compared to what I could earn elsewhere is uncompetitive.

And as a side note, the fixed rate of JetBlue points (about 1.4¢/each) is unimpressive but for most of the attempts I tried to use them throughout the year both domestically and internationally, they proved of little value. A lack of partners is much the same. I looked at a redemption in Mint on my flights to Europe and though I had more than 220,000, it was an insufficient balance for the simple roundtrip. For context, I took United a few years ago on miles and redeemed 160,000 roundtrip (this year was available at 176,000 roundtrip) and multiple times in the last 24 months on American at or around 115,000 roundtrip. Miles aren’t worth enough, they aren’t flexible enough, and there aren’t enough partners to fill gaps in the JetBlue map.

I had higher expectations for JetBlue based on the experiences of my peers. I think its equipment is excellent, but widespread first class availability is a necessity. The limited utility of Move to Mint certificates were the nail in the coffin and the usability of the miles didn’t help. But even then, I really want to love and fly JetBlue, and I am willing to go a little out of my way to use them. But I’m not willing to fly backwards for fewer flights at a higher cost.

#6043. Toxic Lufthansa Plans 1,000 Job Cuts But Cannot Explain Which Jobs Will Go

Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs as management warns that its turnaround is falling short. The financial problems are real, but I am skeptical that another vaguely defined job-cut announcement will help an airline that desperately needs to make peace with its employees in order to ultimately succeed.

According to an internal letter to employees, Lufthansa management plans to cut approximately 1,000 full-time positions across its two main hubs.

The letter, signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and his fellow board members, describes an airline struggling to become competitive. Management reported an adjusted operating loss of €180 million for the first nine months of 2026, an average of €20 million per month. It cited high fuel costs, the Middle East conflict, and nine strike days among the pressures on the business. Management also acknowledged shortcomings in costs, efficiency, and productivity.

But several basic details remain unclear:

(That last point is particularly important)

The pilot union Vereinigung Cockpit responded sharply, accusing management of using an ominous but imprecise announcement to pressure employees as labor negotiations remain unresolved. The union wants answers about which jobs are affected and whether these are additional reductions. It also argues that management must take responsibility for its own operational and strategic decisions.

Ground-staff union Verdi has raised similar concerns. Proposed savings include consolidating technical and administrative work currently performed separately within the organization. There may be a sensible case for that, but telling employees that 1,000 positions will disappear without explaining where or how is an excellent way to spread anxiety far beyond the people ultimately affected…

I keep thinking about my Lufthansa A340-600 flight from Frankfurt to Washington earlier this year.

It was a superb flight, despite a business class seat that was well behind the competition. The improved food and bedding helped, but one of the main reasons I enjoyed it so much was the crew.

The flight attendants were friendly and engaging: the flight attendant working my side was so pleasant. I also sensed pride in delivering the improved onboard service, even though the new service flow created more work.

Those employees gave me a reason to look forward to flying Lufthansa again.

That anecdote certainly does not establish how many employees Lufthansa needs or whether its current labor agreements are sustainable (and this announcement does not suggest any crew positions are being cut). But my experience illustrates something management should remember as it tries to rebuild the business: good employees can make passengers want to come back, even when the seat itself is nothing special. And “happy employees make happy customers” include ground staff, lounge staff, and customer service folks too.

Lufthansa has published its latest proposal to the pilot union, offering the prospect of up to 1,000 cockpit hires by 2033 and up to 150 additional captain promotions annually. In exchange, it seeks changes to compensation and productivity. The proposal also includes one-time payments for 2027 and 2028, with salary increases beginning in 2029.

Those prospective hires are a separate issue from the proposed hub job cuts. The different figures concern different roles and timeframes.

Management should not have to accept every union demand and employees also have an interest in a financially viable airline: reaching an agreement will require concessions. But Lufthansa must find a way to make peace with its workforce. The latest announcement has already inflamed matters, and I struggle to see how leaving so much uncertainty helps either side reach an agreement.

If Lufthansa can eliminate unnecessary duplication while protecting the operation and treating affected employees fairly, it should be clear about it.  I want Lufthansa to succeed. My A340 flight reminded me how good it can be. I would hate to see the enthusiasm I encountered onboard become another casualty of the never-ending conflict between management and labor.

Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time positions in Frankfurt and Munich, but has yet to publicly explain several essential details, including whether those reductions are part of an existing program.

Cost control is necessary, especially as market uncertainty and high oil prices continue. But so is a workforce willing to help deliver the airline that Lufthansa wants passengers to pay a premium to fly. My recent experience demonstrated how much its employees contribute, and I hope management can find a path to profitability that gives those employees a reason to remain invested in its success. Lufthansa is in desperate need of strong leadership…I’ll just leave it at that.
