#6023. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6022. The Best Galapagos Cruises in 2027 That Combine Luxe Amenities With Rugged Adventure

Visiting the Galapagos can feel like stepping onto another planet. This chain of volcanic islands is a mystical realm of otherworldly lava formations, sweeping oceanic vistas, ancient flora, and endemic animal species not found anywhere else on earth.

This unique archipelago of 20 scattered islands—plus dozens more islets and notable rocks in between—is best explored by a specialty cruise. Sailing through the Galapagos Islands allows travelers the ease of navigating to the destination’s smaller locales, getting up close to rare wildlife, and the constant presence of naturalists who can maximize every moment, from pointing out passing marine life to guided stargazing on deck.

The best Galapagos cruises combine tourism with conservation.

The best Galapagos cruises are intimate voyages aboard specialized ships designed to help preserve the islands’ delicate ecosystems. When the day of intrepid exploring is finished, the ship becomes your floating home, offering travelers a serene space to relax and debrief about the wonders you've just experienced. Here’s a look at the best Galapagos cruises to take in 2027, spanning everything from boutique yachts and all-inclusive cruises to top-of-the-line expedition ships.

This article has been updated with new information since its original publication date.

Ecoventura's Theory is not only luxurious, but it welcomes families (with children ages six and up) with open arms.

For an intimate, curated voyage through the Galapagos, you can’t go wrong with an Ecoventura cruise. The line operates three Relais & Chateaux yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which has just 10 staterooms for a total of 20 guests. Each stateroom offers oversized windows and a sleek, modern design.

Travelers can choose between Ecoventura’s two seven-night itineraries: The “Beaches and Bays” voyage visits San Cristobal, Espanola, Floreana, Santa Cruz, Bartolome, and North Seymour Islands, and the “Volcanic Wonders” sailing calls upon more remote locations like Isabela and Fernandina Islands. (There’s also the option to combine both into a 14-night sailing.)

The line’s expedition guides, who are trained in birdwatching, stargazing, and nature photography, escort travelers to notable locations, like the red sand beach on Rabida Island with its flocks of American Flamingos, and the iconic pinnacle rock of Bartolome Island. There’s also kayaking, zodiac rides, and snorkeling among sea turtles, sea lions, reef fish, and more. Scuba divers can board the line’s 16-passenger luxury vessel, Galapagos Sky, for multi-day dive excursions to seek out whale sharks, hammerheads, and manta rays.

Galápagos sea lions, as seen on a cruise

One of the most luxurious options in the Galapagos, Silversea has brought its lavish, all-inclusive concept to the rugged archipelago aboard its destination-specific ship Silver Origin. The all-suite, all-balcony vessel holds 100 passengers and offers butler service in every suite, plus an in-room bar stocked to your preferences. Each suite is ultra-spacious, but the villa category offers sweeping terraces, vast living spaces and dining areas, and a separate bedroom. Elsewhere on the ship are two restaurants, a lounge, spa, fitness center, and stargazing platform— collectively, a promise that passengers will never be bored.

Silversea’s seven-day Galapagos itineraries all sail round-trip from the island of San Cristobal. Depending on the exact sailing, voyages call upon a wide variety of islands, including Isabela, Fernandina, North Seymour, Santa Cruz, Espanola, and more. With the included excursions, guests can explore the lunar landscapes of Isabela’s ancient lava flows, witness the seabird sanctuaries of Prince Philip's Steps, participate in guided nature hikes, deep-water snorkeling, zodiac cruises, and kayaking. Luxe touches, like free expedition gear and unlimited pours of Champagne on board, push the voyages over the top. Plus, Silver Origin’s specialized features—like a dynamic positioning system and advanced propulsion—are easier on the local ecosystem's fragile marine life.

The National Geographic Gemini hosts some of the best Galapagos cruises for bringing kids along.

Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board one of Lindblad Expedition's four Galapagos ships: National Geographic Endeavour II, National Geographic Islander II, National Geographic Gemini, and National Geographic Delfina. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini, which launched in 2025, can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board.

andBeyond's 124-foot expedition yacht Galapagos Explorer

With its 124-foot expedition yacht, Galapagos Explorer, andBeyond offers a truly exclusive experience. The yacht has only six rooms to accommodate 12 guests, and it’s also available for a fully private charter. Across the yacht’s four decks are a hot tub, sun deck, swim deck, as well as indoor and outdoor dining rooms and bars. In the five cabins and one larger suite, passengers will find a warm design accented with an oceanic color palette and natural materials like carved wood accents and indigenous textiles—making the ship feel more like a boutique hotel than a cruise. &Beyond’s seven-day itineraries call upon multiple islands either to the east or west, with a mix of popular and more remote locales, like Genovesa, Bartolome, Santa Cruz, Floreana, Espanola, Isabela, and Santa Fe. Snorkeling, kayaking, guided hikes, and island tours are all part of the daily activities with the expedition team, who can personalize each excursion thanks to the small number of guests on board.

The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare carries 16 passengers and 16 crew members.

The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare is all about bespoke attention. The small vessel carries 16 passengers, with 16 crew members to look after guests’ every need. Within the ship’s elegant interiors are seven cabins with gleaming woodwork, marble-accented bathrooms, and an owner’s suite with multiple bedrooms and living spaces.

Spanning the rest of the yacht’s four decks are a panoramic sundeck, hot tub, and indoor and outdoor dining rooms, where chef Pedro Miguel Schiaffino serves up Peruvian Nikkei-style cuisine. Expect selections like potato llapingachos, tuna crudo, barbecued plantains, and shrimp ceviche created with ingredients sourced from local farmers, fishermen, and other purveyors. The lower-deck swim platform and beach club is the launch point for kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling, or lazy days by the water.

Itineraries cover a wide breadth of islands, from the northern reaches of Genovesa to the southernmost Espanola, and Santa Fe, Santa Cruz, and Santiago in between. Western-focused itineraries arc around the far West side of Isabela Island, which allows for rarefied activities. Guests can hike among the penguin colonies and lava rocks of Punta Moreno, as well as the saltwater Darwin Lake located inside of a volcanic crater at Caleta Tagus.

Ecuadorian-owned, family-run expedition line Quasar operates 8-day and 15-day safari-style itineraries that focus on facilitating meaningful wildlife encounters for the small group of guests on board. With these immersive sailings, you might be swimming with sea turtles one day and cruising on a Zodiac boat amid a pod of dolphins the next. The line’s two yachts are designed for intimate trips, carrying a maximum of 32 guests. The 16-passenger Grace yacht has an especially intriguing history: Grace Kelly, who used it for her honeymoon in 1956, and has since been carefully restored to its original opulent glory. Guests can even stay in the revamped Grace Kelly suite, where the iconic actress spent her two-week honeymoon. Both yachts offer modern amenities like oversized hot tubs, al-fresco bars and lounges, sun decks, and more. Everything from meals to shore excursions to the open bar is included in the cruise fare.

Guests also have onboard access to kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling equipment for interacting directly with marine life like reef sharks, sea lions, and marine iguanas whenever the mood strikes. With such a small group, tours are immersive and personalized. Travelers can expect daily Zodiac landings across remote sites on islands like Espanola, Genovesa, Fernandina, Isabela, and Bartolome with expert naturalist guides.

While Flora can fit up to 100 passengers on board, excursions are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer.

Sailing aboard the purpose-built ship Celebrity Flora strikes a perfect balance between relaxing on a luxurious floating resort and chasing the thrill of an adventurous expedition. The all-suite, all-veranda ship offers each guest a personal suite attendant, menus curated by a Michelin-starred chef, and an all-inclusive policy that covers drinks, meals, shore excursions, and even flights. Travelers can also expect a personal touch from crew, with 100 passengers on board and excursions that are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer. Tours included memorable experiences like walks through lava tunnels, panga boat rides along rocky shorelines teeming with Galapagos penguins and sea lions, guided hikes to see blue-footed boobies, frigate birds, giant tortoises, rare flora, and ancient cacti.

Opportunities to spot diverse wildlife don’t end once travelers return to the ship. Celebrity Flora is outfitted with Sky Suites featuring the line’s signature Infinite Veranda that brings the extraordinary outdoor surroundings directly into your room. The window transforms into an open-air veranda at the touch of a button, allowing travelers to fully immerse themselves in the wondrous landscapes without even leaving their room. Plus, features like solar panels, reverse-osmosis water filtration, and dynamic positioning are gentle on the islands’ precious resources.

How early should I book a Galapagos cruise?

For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then.

Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee).

When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands?

With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands.

The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s.

What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise?

The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands.

#6021. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6020. The Best Places to Go in Asia in 2027

It’s that time of year when we drop our expert-curated list of the best places to go in Asia in 2027. But before we do, we have to acknowledge that 2026 was a challenging year across the continent. Amid a shifting geopolitical environment and climate change events, there is now a renewed sense of purpose as communities across Asia look at art, food, and nature for a brighter 2027.

Our list of the best places to go in Asia in 2027 showcases the sheer diversity of experiences on offer for every kind of traveler. For the outdoorsy, new long distance hiking trails in the Caucasus, via ancient wine caves and Silk Road-era caravansaries, take you deep into Armenia’s history. Tourists will always flock to Japan’s glittering megacities, but on their outskirts—like in Niigata Prefecture just two hours from Tokyo—regenerative tourism models like the Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale draw visitors into the country’s stunning rural landscapes.

Penang is a foodie favorite, and 2027 brings a clutch of revamped stays and inventive new restaurants spotlighting heritage ingredients. Further afield in the Philippines, the emerging slow-food culture in Negros Occidental is worth planning a trip around.

For that vibrant city energy, 2027 is a big year, as Jaipur celebrates its 300th anniversary with a year-round calendar of commemorative events. Bangkok has a whole roster of buzzy new hotel openings lined up, while Shanghai is set to see a culture-filled year with the biennale and new museums along the waterfront. From skyscraper-dotted metropolises to remote landscapes sustained by community initiatives, Asia gives everyone a reason to visit in 2027. —Malavika Bhattacharya

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: nature, history, and slow travel on foot

Amernia's Transcaucasian Trail is dotted with monasteries, ancient caves, and roadside inns—and in 2027, it will feel even easier to tackle thanks to new maps, updated trail sections, and trekking services.

Built among the peaks and valleys of the Caucasus, Armenia’s ancient roots and mountainous landscapes reward slow travel. Along the country’s two long-distance trails, the Armenian National Trail (ANT) and the Transcaucasian Trail (TCT), medieval monasteries rise above dramatic gorges, Silk Road-era caravansaries dot historic mountain routes, and ancient caves recall thousands of years of winemaking history. In Yerevan, one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, historic fortresses and pale pink stone buildings sit side by side with a colorful café and restaurant scene.

In 2027, Armenia's growing outdoor scene makes it especially exciting for adventurous travelers. The TCT, which will eventually span nearly 1,900 miles across Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan, is becoming easier to tackle with new downloadable maps, updated trail sections and signage, and trekking services offering itinerary planning and luggage transfers. The Armenian section of the TCT extends from Arevik National Park in the south, past Syunik’s cave dwellings and the Tatev Monastery, rising against deep river gorges; through the volcanic massifs of the Gegham Mountains, the forests of Dilijan National Park, and ending at Lake Arpi National Park near Georgia.

Meanwhile, the ANT, a 620-mile network that will eventually connect more than 100 villages, opened its first sections in June 2026 with more to open next year. Trails currently extend through Tavush and Lori, and soon Vayots Dzor, where visitors can birdwatch in alpine steppes, stay with families, and cook herb-filled meals with local hosts, while sampling lavash (Armenia's UNESCO-listed flatbread) baked in a deep, clay oven, and regional bounties like forest berries, mushrooms, cornelian cherry, and rosehip soup. Collectively, the trails offer a new way to experience Armenia's landscapes and communities on foot. —Alicia Erickson

Go for: a luxury and lifestyle hotel boom reshaping the city

Golden hour in Bangkok Yai's historic canal district, beneath the towering Wat Paknam Big Buddha, showcases the bustling city's eternal allure.

Already one of the world’s most-visited cities, Bangkok is giving travelers new reasons to return in 2027. A remarkable wave of hotel openings is part of a broader luxury boom sweeping the Thai capital, which ranked fourth globally for new luxury store openings in 2025. There’s been a recent influx of designer flagships, including Gucci's renovated and reopened boutique, Ralph Lauren’s concept store at Central Embassy, and Acne Studios at Siam Paragon.

Bangkok is also expanding its world-class dining, contemporary art, and urban green spaces, while preserving the street stalls, markets, and neighborhood restaurants that made it famous. It now has nine restaurants on Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list, more than any other city in the region, with acclaimed newcomers, such as the reopening of Sra Bua by Num Weerawat at Siam Kempinski Hotel Bangkok, and a growing natural wine scene.

The city’s hotel boom spans luxury, lifestyle, and design. Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026, while Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit; The Langham, Custom House, Bangkok; and YOTEL Bangkok Sukhumvit are accepting reservations for later in the year. Other 2027 openings include Conrad Bangkok Sukhumvit Queen's Park, the renowned Siam Motors Building, which is transforming into the Siam Pan Pacific Bangkok, Pan Pacific Serviced Suites Bangkok, and Hotel Indigo by IHG. There have also been rumblings that Belmond’s luxury Eastern and Oriental Express will return to Bangkok in 2027.

The Green Bangkok 2030 Project—an urban plan to increase Bangkok's green spaces to 110 square feet per person—helped drive the 2026 reopening of the mile-long Green Bridge, a car-free greenway connecting Lumpini Park and Benjakitti Park. Song Wat Road has emerged as a modern cultural hub—with famed street food, an array of art spaces, artisan coffee shops, and vintage clothing—amid expanded plans to transform Chinatown.

The December 2025 opening of Dib Bangkok, Thailand’s first museum devoted exclusively to international contemporary art, was another significant milestone. Australia’s Museum of Old and New Art has also announced plans for a Bangkok outpost, further strengthening the city’s reputation as a serious art destination. —Kaila Yu

Go for: the Pink City’s 300th anniversary

Old becomes new in Jaipur, which celebrates its 300th year as a city in 2027. The opulent Sarvato Jaipur (pictured), for example, was once a terrace pavilion used for an audience with the maharaja.

In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II established Jaipur as the capital of his kingdom, envisioning it as a financial and artistic hub. As the city marks its 300th year in 2027, the City Palace—the current residence of the erstwhile royals—readies for the occasion with new exhibits across its galleries, as well as in private spaces not usually accessible to the public. Traces of Us, an exhibit by the Jaipur Centre for Art, marks the anniversary with contemporary works by artists like M.F. Husain and Bharti Kher displayed across the palace. A terrace pavilion once used for an audience with the maharaja is now the stylish, open-air restaurant the Sarvato, where Sawai Padmanabh Singh partners with hotelier Abhishek Honawar to showcase a modern, six-course menu championing both the everyday and the celebratory food of Rajasthan, served with a spectacular view of Jaipur.

Honawar, best known for his boutique Michelin Key property the Johri, a restored 19th-century haveli in the Old City, added three more suites this year to the hotel’s original five keys. Set to open later in 2026 is Hawa Haveli, an eight-key stay with a restaurant and cocktail bar, housed in a 19th-century merchant mansion—another intimate boutique property from the same team.

For three days in December 2026, the Jaigarh Heritage Festival brings folk artists and craftspeople to the 11th-century Jaigarh Fort to celebrate the city’s 300th anniversary, while the Jaipur Literature Festival in January brings the stalwarts of the literary world to the Pink City.

A themed walk, Jaipur 300: A City of Craft and Courtyards, led by Neeraj Chauhan of Jaipurnama, traces three centuries of living heritage. And to carry a piece of Jaipur back with you, the Jaipur Watch Company has released two special timepieces inspired by the City Palace’s beautiful Leheriya Gate and Peacock Gate. —Shalbha Sarda

Go for: slow food culture, heritage ingredients, and eco-friendly experiences

The 18-villa Manami Resort in Sipalay offers a conservation-first stay that connects visitors to the surrounding landscape.

Cooking at fish farm 7 Hectares, which uses hyperlocal ingredients, is a way to tap into Negros Occidental's slow-food movement.

Formerly home to wealthy sugar barons and sprawling plantations, the 19th-century beginnings of industrialized sugar production, today Negros Occidental is at the heart of a thriving slow-food scene. In 2027, this Negros Island province, 330 miles south of the Philippines capital Manila, will play host to the prestigious triennial Organic World Congress, as well as the returning Terra Madre Asia and Pacific slow-food festival.

In the biennale’s first iteration, Michelin-starred chefs appeared alongside local producers like Francisco “Kiko” Torno, owner of 7 Hectares fish farm, whose pop-up kitchen serves slow-food dishes cooked with hyperlocal ingredients. And he’s not the only one: The island’s farmers, fishermen, cooks, and chefs are all determined to champion the homegrown, and many welcome visitors on local food tours.

A short boat ride off the coast takes nature lovers to the award-winning Suyac Island Mangrove Eco-Park, which is expected to be nominated for the prestigious ASEAN Sustainable Community-Based Tourism Award in 2027. Islanders guide visitors through an old mangrove forest with giant fruit bats, navigated by wooden walkways, telling stories about their community. Stay at conservation-first Manami Resort in Sipalay, which joined the Michelin hotels list in May 2026, and has 18 villas, each with its own “nature butler,” and a marine biologist to help guests to tune into their environment. —Claire Turrell

Go for: landscapes reimagined through art

The Hoshitoge terraced rice fields, fed by Niigata’s winter snowmelt, still yield an abundant harvest each autumn. It is here, in these zones between human settlements and mountain landscapes—known as satoyama in Japanese—that Niigata's beauty shines.

Travel in Japan is no longer just about the big cities. For travelers interested in sustainable tourism, the focus is shifting to rural areas, such as Niigata Prefecture on Japan’s west coast, just two hours from Tokyo. In Japan, “satoyama” describes the transition zones between human settlements (sato) and mountain landscapes (yama), where communities have traditionally managed forests and farmland in harmony with nature. As rural populations decline, these cultural landscapes are disappearing, but in Niigata, the Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale has emerged as a model for regenerative tourism. Returning for its 10th edition in July 2027, the contemporary art festival uses creativity to revive the region.

Spanning Tokamachi and Tsunan in southern Niigata, Echigo-Tsumari is a vast landscape of rice terraces, forests, and villages. The triennale brings large-scale works by Japanese and international artists into abandoned buildings and open spaces—from MAD Architects’ immersive Tunnel of Light in Kiyotsu Gorge to Christian Boltanski’s meditative The Last Class inside a shuttered school—while bringing revenue to depopulated villages. Locals are involved as guides and hosts, ensuring income stays within the community.

At a time when overtourism is challenging Japan’s hotspots, the festival demonstrates how cultural tourism can support rural communities off the beaten track. This ethos extends to Niigata’s hospitality scene. In June 2026, NIPPONIA Niigata Furumachi Hanamachi transformed three historic buildings in Niigata City’s geisha district into a dispersed hotel. Guests are encouraged to treat the entire neighborhood as the hotel and take part in cultural experiences such as geisha performances. Yadoya Dōmichi, a similar dispersed-hotel concept in the mountains outside Itoigawa that accepts just one group per night, opened in January 2026 and offers guests the chance to join in with everyday village activities such as planting rice in spring and building snow huts in winter. —Karen Gardiner

Go for: new ways to explore the island’s cultural and culinary heritage

Root House by Gēn is one of several Penang restaurants embracing the city's culinary roots anew.

Soori Penang, a shophouse-turned-hotel, is a star example of how the city's historic buildings have been given a second life.

Penang’s kopitiams, hawker centers, and beloved nasi kandar joints culminate in a layered culinary landscape which, like its styles of architecture and sites of worship, reflects over two centuries worth of maritime trade, British colonialism, and waves of settlers from China, India, and beyond. Now, a clutch of chefs are spinning modern takes on heritage produce. At newcomer Root House by Gēn, chef-founder Johnson Wong interprets the movement of people from China to Malaysia into a menu that presents traditional ingredients like century egg and fermented bean curd in a fine-dining format.

Within the mural-lined streets of George Town, historic shophouses-turned-hotels offer firsthand immersion into the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Newcomer Soori Penang is noteworthy as it was driven by a deeply personal restoration mission: Architect Soo K. Chan once called the now-converted shophouses home. Part of the Leading Hotels of the World, it resides alongside the 175-year-old Khoo Kongsi clan house and will soon unveil the three-bedroom Clan House Suite as well as a cigar and whiskey lounge. The Qing Suites, meanwhile, is a forgotten 1904 annex within the Cheong Fatt Tze or The Blue Mansion of Crazy Rich Asians fame. Once housing the servants’ quarters, it now stands as a 13-suite boutique property on the historic Lebuh Leith.

A brainchild of Hong Kong actress Amy Yip, Penang’s affinity for durian will translate to the world’s first durian-themed luxury hotel, complete with private tasting lounge, expected to debut in late 2027.

In early 2027, the popular Gurney Drive Hawker Center will relocate to Gurney Bay, an expansive promenade and public park facing the Andaman Sea. Further afield, a new cable car at Penang Hill, a UNESCO-designated biosphere reserve, will both serve as an additional tourist attraction and alleviate the strain on the century-old funicular that ascends to its peak, 2,700 feet above sea level. Operations are set to begin in late 2027. —Samia Qaiyum

Go for: a tropical island transforming ahead of the global spotlight

The wellness-focused Regent Phú Quốc shows how this destination has become one of Southeast Asia's fastest growing resort hubs—and 2027 is the year to reap the benefits for yourself.

Phú Quốc has transformed over the past decade from a sleepy fishing island into one of Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing resort hubs. White-sand beaches and fishing villages still edge an interior blanketed by protected rainforest parks, but increasingly share space with resorts and entertainment complexes. Now, another transformation is underway as the island prepares to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November 2027.

The scale alone is dramatic: SOM is designing a waterfront district with an 800,000-square-foot convention center and performance arena. Phú Quốc International Airport is expanding toward a capacity of 24 million passengers annually, while homegrown Sun PhuQuoc Airways builds connections across Asia. Thousands of hotel rooms are coming, too, with Rixos, the Luxury Collection, JW Marriott Marquis, Moxy, and Conrad among some of the many openings slated over the next year.

For all the development, there are still quieter corners—whether kayaking mangrove-lined waterways in the north or checking into the pleasantly understated, wellness-centric Regent Phu Quoc. But this is also a place to surrender to spectacle: soar over turquoise waters on an 6-mile cable car or catch the nightly extravaganza of lasers, acrobatics, and pyrotechnics at the Kiss of the Sea show. —Dan Q. Dao

Go for: a revitalized waterfront best explored on foot

Snøhetta's Shanghai Grand Opera House venue and landmark, which opened in October 2026, illustrates the cultural revolution stirring within the city.

China’s trading powerhouse, Shanghai, sits on the Huangpu River, a commercial lifeline dividing the city, and home to its most famous waterside promenade, the Bund. South along the river, the 16th Shanghai Biennale will open in November 2027 at the Power Station of Art, a contemporary art museum crowned with a 540-foot chimney.

In the West Bund, a former industrial waterfront turned arts district, where more museums are joining its riverside row, the annual West Bund Art and Design fair will draw galleries from across Asia and beyond in the same weeks.

On the river’s opposite shore, in Houtan, Snøhetta's Shanghai Grand Opera House opened in October 2026. It’s a world-class venue for the performing arts and a civic landmark in its own right: a spiraling ramp climbs the fan-shaped roof to a terrace open to all, with Expo Culture Park spread out below.

Shanghai’s hotel landscape is also shifting in 2027. Fairmont Peace Hotel, Victor Sassoon’s art deco creation, and Bund landmark dating to 1929, which once welcomed film star Charlie Chaplin and playwright Noël Coward, is due to reopen as Raffles Peace Hotel Shanghai, with its “historic treasures” preserved. And on the North Bund, a disused office block facing the Bund across the water becomes Lux's first Shanghai hotel, Lux On the Bund, with 100 river-view rooms. —Yolaine Feng

Go for: a regional food and wine scene, with ancient landscapes and new hotels

To appreciate Yunnan in 2027, pair the buzzy city energy of Kunming, which has turned into a destination in its own right, with serene countrysides accessible via towns like Lijiang, where the Amandayan (pictured) is based.

China, as it appears on our TikTok and Instagram feeds, is all gleaming skyscrapers, driverless cars, and neon-lit megacities. Yunnan, in China’s southwest, offers another view: a part of the country where those same advances exist alongside snowcapped mountains, ancient tea forests, highland lakes, and villages tucked into valleys. Start in Kunming, the provincial capital. Long regarded as a gateway to the rest of Yunnan, the city has become a destination in its own right. Here in Spring City a few experiences are essential, like digging into crossing-the-bridge noodles (guòqiáo mǐxiàn) and wandering the Dounan flower market, one of the largest in Asia. There are also new restaurants and bars giving the city fresh energy—and many of which have Yunnan wine now appearing on their menus (Shangri-La’s high-altitude wines, in particular, are starting to make a name for themselves in China). For a taste of the new, book a table at Yijin Sting or Cui House, both of which pair contemporary Yunnanese cooking with local pours. Between meals, the new Cuihu Urban Greenway, opened in 2025, makes it easier to explore the city center on foot; it connects Cuihu Lake with Kunming Old Street, which boasts museums, cafés, and historic façades. The hotel scene is kicking up too: Shangri-La Kunming opened in 2026 with an immersive local tea experience.

Kunming is just the starting point. From there, head west to the city of Dali, where the Cangshan mountains rise behind the old city and Erhai Lake stretches out beyond it. The Three Pagodas have stood at the foot of the mountains for more than a thousand years. Mostly, though, Dali is a place to slow down—and the Dali Edition hotel, opened in June 2026, caters to travelers who wish to do so.

Further flung are destinations like Lijiang, with a charming Old Town and easy access to the scenic Blue Moon Valley. Between Lijiang and Shangri-La lies Tiger Leaping Gorge, where the Jinsha River squeezes between the over-three-mile-high mountains, where one- and two-day treks are well worth the effort. Shangri-La, at the northern end of the trip, is largely Tibetan in culture: Time your visit to Songzanlin Monastery for the morning chants, then spend a late afternoon in Dukezong Ancient Town before walking up the hill to the giant prayer wheel, where you can join locals in spinning it. Yunnan promises much to explore—and rewards those willing to dig deep into its reaches. —Ali Farooqui

#6019. American Unveils Limited-Edition Jacket Made of Recycled Aircraft Seats

American Airlines is joining in the “Cyber Week” shopping holiday with the planned release of a branded jacket made from reclaimed leather from the carrier’s old aircraft, including the McDonnell Douglas MD-80.

The special, limited-edition MA-1 flight jackets are made by Alpha Industries and come with an American patch celebrating the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

The airline plans to make 10 jackets available for purchase each day from Nov. 30 through Dec. 4, at the price of 200,000 AAdvantage miles each.

Alpha Industries said it received 650 seats from American for the project. Each jacket requires 10 to 12 seats to make, depending on the quality of the material.

American is also advertising its other branded merchandise ahead of the holidays, including suitcases and limited-edition pickleball paddles made in collaboration with Volair.

From Nov. 27 through Dec. 2, AAdvantage members can save up to 50% when purchasing 500,000 or more miles.

#6018. Cayman Airways Adds New Route to U.S.

Cayman Airways will launch a new seasonal service to the U.S. next year.

Starting May 21, 2027, the carrier will connect Grand Cayman and Nashville, Tennessee. Flights will operate twice per week, on Mondays and Fridays, through Aug. 16.

Tickets will become available for purchase early next month, officials said.

Cayman Airways is the flag carrier of the Cayman Islands and has its main hub at Owen Roberts International Airport in Grand Cayman.

Its current U.S. destinations are Miami, Tampa, Florida, Austin, Texas, Denver, and Los Angeles.

#6015. BermudAir Adds 10 New Destinations, 18 New Routes

Bermudian flag carrier BermudAir will nearly double its U.S. footprint next year as it launches new connections across North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The carrier announced Tuesday that it will serve New Orleans; Nashville, Tennessee; New Haven, Connecticut; Burlington, Vermont; Portland, Maine; San Antonio; New Brunswick, Canada; Ocho Rios, Jamaica; San Salvador, El Salvador; and San Pedro Sula, Honduras, for the first time.

Accompanying the 10 new destinations are 18 new routes. BermudAir is also moving to expand service to existing markets, such as Bermuda, Anguilla, Belize, Grand Cayman, Guatemala, and Turks and Caicos.

“From New Orleans and Nashville to San Antonio and New England, we’re seeing tremendous interest in what BermudAir offers,” founder and CEO Adam Scott said in a news release.

BermudAir currently serves eight U.S. cities, all on or close to the East Coast, and three destinations in Canada. Its main hub is L.F. Wade International Airport in St. George’s, Bermuda.

Generally, you won’t want to transfer your points or miles unless you have a specific redemption in mind. #6013. FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

Air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA said, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

“Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”

The FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

#6012. Atmos For Business: Earn Up To 23.5x Points On Alaska & Hawaiian Flights

Atmos for Business is the small business rewards program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, and it runs parallel to the Atmos Rewards program (Atmos for Business used to be known as the EasyBiz program).

Most major US airlines have a small business rewards program, and the intent is to offer extra rewards when businesses book travel. The good news is that even small businesses qualify for this, and it can really boost the rewards you earn.

Along those lines, in light of the recent refresh of the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card (learn more), I think this program is worth a close look. Long story short, Atmos Rewards members could be earning up to 23.5x points per dollar spent on airfare. Based on my valuation of 1.5 cents per Atmos Rewards point, that’s the equivalent of a jaw dropping 35.25% return on eligible spending. That’s simply unrivaled.

Atmos for Business is the self-managed business travel program by Alaska and Hawaiian, intended for small and medium sized businesses.

The program is open to companies and organizations with at least $5,000 in annual travel spending, so if you’re a frequent flyer with the company and have a small business, that’s not much of a hurdle. You can add an unlimited number of employees to your account, and all of their spending counts toward that requirement.

Now, the terms suggest that you must have spent at least $5,000 or more on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian travel in the last 15 months, though in practice, that’s not directly enforced, best I can tell. After all, this is even intended to attract new businesses that may be looking to switch travel to Alaska or Hawaiian.

When a business enrolls in Atmos for Business, it’s assigned a company Atmos Rewards loyalty number. Atmos for Business then offers an impressive number of bonus rewards:

Beyond increased loyalty benefits for the business, Atmos for Business offers a platform that is supposed to make booking easier, with features like the following:

The total number of points that you can earn per dollar spent with Atmos for Business is pretty incredible, assuming you have the Atmos Rewards Business Card. As of 2027, Atmos Rewards members can choose how they get rewarded for flying, and they can choose to earn rewards based on distance flown, dollars spent, or segments flown.

Assuming you choose to earn based on how much you spend, here’s how the math works out:

As you can see, a non-elite member booking through the Atmos for Business portal and paying with the Atmos Rewards Business Card would earn 15x points per dollar spent, while a Titanium member booking through the Atmos for Business portal and paying with the Atmos Rewards Business Card would earn 22.5x points.

This doesn’t factor in the extra 1x points that the company earns, for a total of up to 23.5x points per dollar spent. Furthermore, it doesn’t factor in the 10% status points bonus, but that’s a different story.

While I’m going for top tier Atmos Rewards Titanium status, I still don’t fly with Alaska or Hawaiian often, given that I live in Miami, so it’s not the most practical carrier. Still, my goodness, the return on airfare spending is absolutely unreal here, if you are a loyalist.

To make sure there wasn’t any catch to all of this, I signed up for the Atmos for Business program. This was super straightforward — I just had to log into my Atmos Rewards account, and then fill out some basic company details.

This included the country my business is registered in, my business name, my tax ID, my phone number, and my address.

It was that easy, and I was registered instantly. The Atmos for Business program account management page looked mighty familiar, as it’s basically the same concept as the American AAdvantage Business program. There you can add travelers, manage payments, etc.

To actually book travel, you just select the “Book Travel” heading. That will bring you to a search that looks identical to what you’ll find on Alaska’s website, but it’s customized to Atmos for Business.

Pricing is identical to what you’d find directly on the websites of Alaska or Hawaiian, so that’s pretty tough to beat.

Atmos for Business is the small business rewards program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. Even small businesses qualify, though the idea is that it’s for those who spend at least $5,000 per year on flights with the company across employees, which isn’t a very high bar.

The main advantage of Atmos for Business is that you earn one extra point per dollar spent, plus 10% bonus status points. But the area where the program gets really rewarding is if you have the Atmos Rewards Business Card, as that offers 10x points per dollar spent through Atmos for Business.

If you were an Atmos Rewards Titanium member booking through Atmos for Business and paying with the Atmos Rewards Business Card, you’d potentially earn a total of 23.5x points per dollar spent on airfare, with no caps. This is simply an amazing rate of return. Man, I’m really bummed that I can’t fly with Alaska or Hawaiian more, as that return on spending is something to get excited about.

What do you make of the Atmos for Business program?

The real-world value of choosing the right credit cards for your everyday spending We frequently tout the incredible value you can get from top rewards credit cards — from bonus categories to welcome offers, lucrative benefits to monthly statement credits.

But exactly how much value can you get from matching the right credit cards to your spending habits?

Well, we recently set out to answer this very question.

We challenged three American households with a simple question: Can you make the money you’re already spending work harder for you?

Mollie and Kevin were up first. The pair recently moved in together ahead of their wedding, and they’re working through how to combine their finances while also saving for their dream honeymoon to Thailand and Vietnam. Both had travel rewards cards before the challenge, but they weren’t coordinating their purchases.

Plus, they were still using debit cards for some everyday expenses.

In short, they had room for improvement in how they made the most of the cards in their wallets.

They started by sitting down to map out their spending habits, which uncovered three primary categories being spread across multiple cards, without any rhyme or reason:

Plus, they had some major wedding expenses coming up, which gave them a great opportunity to snag a new card with a lucrative welcome bonus.

By coordinating their household spending, closing duplicate cards and opening a new one for the welcome offer, they’re now earning more from the same purchases they were already making.

The remaining balance of the catering bill for their wedding alone hit the minimum spending required to earn the welcome offer, and when all was said and done, the couple took home 120,000 points — worth nearly $2,500 based on TPG’s most recent valuations.

Next stop for Mollie and Kevin? Southeast Asia.

Next, we meet Amy, a single mom of two daughters in Maryland. She’s been earning rewards on her favorite hotel cobranded card for years, using it for basically every purchase she could — from utilities to groceries to clothing. She’s racked up nearly 400,000 points in the process, which have come in handy as her daughters have begun traveling for dance competitions.

However, she was concerned her hotel loyalty meant she was sacrificing some value. Could she shift some of her spending to a new card to diversify her rewards?

With back-to-school shopping and dance classes making up the bulk of her spending in the next month, she opted to add a new card to her wallet that offered solid rewards on all purchases — along with some easy-to-use statement credits.

And a large home repair bill accelerated her progress toward earning the welcome bonus — a great way to make the best of an unexpected expense.

She’s still keeping her old hotel card open, since it features a low annual fee, and she’ll still want to earn (and redeem) those points when it works. However, the rewards on her new card give her the newfound flexibility she didn’t have originally.

“I really had tunnel vision with the hotel points,” she admitted. “I was leaving money on the table."

Our final household focuses on Denver, a travel enthusiast who was thrown a pair of major life curveballs last year when her grandfather passed away, and her mom lost her job (and thus her source of income). She moved back home to help, and travel (understandably) shifted to the back burner.

While Denver charged many purchases to her favorite travel rewards card, she had other purchases pulled straight from her bank account. She was also worried that putting everything on her credit card would encourage her to spend more. However, there was a key opportunity in her new role as a caretaker: focusing on everyday spending rather than travel rewards.

Denver opted for a new cash-back credit card with bonuses at grocery stores, on streaming services and at gas stations. It even offered a one-time $300 cash-back bonus. These rewards can immediately help offset her household bills, like medication costs, be saved for an unexpected expense, or even go toward a future getaway with her family.

She’s continuing to pay her statement balance in full and on time, so it’s not about spending more; it’s about smarter spending based on her current situation.

After just a month, Denver is tracking toward nearly $1,500 in cash-back rewards in the first year — just by being more intentional with her everyday spending.

One of the most common questions we get here at TPG is, “What’s the best credit card for me?” And there’s a simple answer: “It depends.”

Everyone’s situation is unique, so there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to maximizing your everyday spending. And these three households demonstrate that exact phenomenon.

One went with a new travel card to maximize their wedding purchases. Another opted for a flexible rewards card to diversify her earnings. And the third focused on a cash-back card to support her family’s bottom line.

All of them are now getting even more value from the purchases they were already making.

This is the power of matching the cards in your wallet to your daily spending — while keeping a keen eye on earning the rewards that work best for you.

Don’t miss out on the chance to make your everyday purchases work harder for you. Analyze where you’re spending your money today, so you can unlock even more value tomorrow.

#6010. FAA Bans Line Up And Wait Operations “Forever,” With Even More Delays Expected

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has introduced stricter requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations at airports across the United States, effective November 24, 2026. The new rules require a dedicated air traffic control supervisor to oversee these operations, potentially preventing controllers at understaffed facilities from using the procedure. The change comes just as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, raising concerns about longer departure queues and additional flight delays.

Despite reports describing the measure as a permanent nationwide ban, the FAA has not prohibited Line Up and Wait operations altogether. Instead, it has made them conditional on additional staffing, introducing another operational challenge for an air traffic control system already struggling with personnel shortages.

The new requirement is outlined in FAA Notice JO 7210.979, which mandates that a standalone watch supervision position must be staffed whenever Line Up and Wait operations are conducted. Previously, the relevant guidance recommended that the local control position should not be combined with other responsibilities. The updated wording makes this a mandatory requirement, meaning supervisors can no longer simultaneously perform other operational duties while overseeing these operations.

Line Up and Wait is a widely used air traffic control procedure that allows aircraft to enter an assigned runway and hold in position while waiting for takeoff clearance. It helps improve runway efficiency because departing aircraft are already positioned when the runway becomes available. However, under the new requirements, airports without sufficient personnel to provide dedicated supervision will have to keep aircraft waiting at taxiway holding points instead. This could reduce departure capacity, particularly during busy periods.

The timing is concerning because November 24 coincides with the beginning of one of America's busiest Thanksgiving travel periods. According to the FAA forecast reported by Traveling for Business, more than 52,000 flights were scheduled for that Tuesday, with over 417,000 expected throughout the nine-day holiday period.

FAA provided a statement to Simple Flying to clarify the new rule:

The FAA is taking proactive steps to further strengthen runway safety by enhancing staffing and supervisory requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) at airports nationwide, effective Nov. 24, 2026. These measures ensure dedicated controller staffing and supervisory oversight during LUAW operations and reinforce the FAA’s commitment to maintaining the highest safety standards. This will not impact airport operations.

Dedicated Local Control: The local control position responsible for arriving and departing aircraft must not be combined with any non-local control position.

Stand-Alone Watch Supervision: A dedicated watch supervision position must be staffed and cannot be combined with any other position. This strengthens existing guidance by making stand-alone watch supervision mandatory.

The controversy gained attention after a radio exchange at Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ). According to TheTravel, a controller told a Southwest Airlines crew about the new nationwide requirement, warning it could slow departures during the busiest travel time of the Thanksgiving rush. The controller described the restriction as something that would last forever, although the FAA's official notice did not use that wording.

Importantly, the FAA's stated objective is to improve runway safety, not reduce airport capacity. Having a dedicated supervisor overseeing operations should help prevent distractions and improve situational awareness when aircraft are positioned on active runways. The FAA's existing procedures also emphasize that Line Up and Wait is not takeoff clearance and that aircraft should not normally remain in that position for more than 90 seconds without further instructions.

But there is also an important clarification: the official notice lists June 9, 2027, as its cancellation date. Therefore, describing the measure as an indefinite or permanent prohibition is misleading. The actual impact will depend on staffing levels at individual towers and how frequently they can provide the additional supervisory position.

FAA ties delayed pay to efficiency metrics that demand more on position time amid a 3,000 controller shortfall.

The FAA is attempting to address its longstanding air traffic controller shortage through an ambitious recruitment campaign, including an unusual effort to attract video gamers. In October 2026, the agency announced that it had hired 2,235 controller trainees during the fiscal year, exceeding its recruitment target. The campaign reportedly attracted more than 12,000 qualified applicants within just 24 hours, demonstrating the potential of targeting candidates with strong multitasking and decision-making abilities.

However, recruiting additional candidates does not immediately solve the staffing problem. According to the FAA's 2026 workforce plan, becoming a fully certified controller can take more than two years, depending on the complexity of the assigned facility. The agency has set recruitment targets of 2,300 trainees for fiscal year 2027 and 2,400 for 2028, while expanding training capacity and modernizing its workforce management procedures.

As a result, the new Line Up and Wait requirements could create additional operational pressure before the benefits of increased recruitment become apparent. Although the measure is intended to strengthen runway safety, airports with limited staffing may have fewer opportunities to use an efficiency-enhancing procedure. For Thanksgiving travelers, the immediate concern is that an already busy aviation network could face additional departure bottlenecks during the holiday rush.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6009. Awful: American Dies After Picking Fight With MMA Fighter At Bangkok Hotel

An American who was reportedly yelling at staff at a hotel in Thailand ended up picking a fight with the wrong guest, and it ended up costing him his life. This is both tragic and insanely irresponsible on both sides… I just don’t get what people are thinking sometimes…

Media in Thailand is reporting on an incident that happened early this morning (Sunday, November 22, 2026), whereby a 46-year-old American tourist died at a hotel in Bangkok’s Phra Khanong area, after an altercation with a 39-year-old Italian man, who was reportedly an MMA fighter.

According to the initial police report, the American had been arguing loudly with the hotel staff at the reception desk, for reasons that are unclear as of now. As an Italian hotel guest walked past him and attempted to enter an elevator, the American reportedly grabbed him and pulled him out.

The confrontation escalated, and turned into a physical struggle, during which the Italian man placed the American man in a chokehold, until he lost consciousness. Hotel staff called emergency services, and while first responders performed CPR, the American couldn’t be revived. Police also found an abrasion on the victim’s forehead.

The Italian man remained at the scene, and told authorities that he had been acting in self-defense, after being attacked. Police took him into custody, and he potentially faces manslaughter charges, though the case is still being investigated.

The hotel at which this incident happened hasn’t yet been named, but this occurred at Sukhumvit Soi 48 — there are several hotels in that area, with the biggest “brand name” property being a Ramada Plaza by Wyndham.

I feel horribly for the family of the person who lost his life. I would have to imagine that odds are high that there were likely some substances involved here, and that this all happened after a big Saturday night out. After all, most people aren’t looking to get into a massive fight while getting their first cup of coffee in the morning (or maybe it’s just me?).

But my gosh, the “victim” here sounds like he was acting absolutely horribly, arguing with hotel staff, and then picking a fight with a random person. At the same time, that also doesn’t justify the response of getting into a conflict that leads to a fatality.

I absolutely love Thailand — the people are so friendly, the food is amazing, and the country also offers such diversity in terms of landscape, whether you want a city, a jungle, or a beach. However, there’s also no denying that the country (and particularly Bangkok) attracts a large percentage of tourists who are looking for debauchery.

None of this has anything to do with a conflict that gets to the point of costing someone their life, but I can’t help but mention that when I review hotels, I tend to take a lot of pictures in lobbies around 4-5AM, when it’s the emptiest (since I’m a morning person anyway). Virtually everywhere else in the world, there’s not a single soul awake in public. Bangkok is probably the one exception, where you see a countless number of people moving through lobbies, elevators, etc., engaged in various forms of “business.”

An American man lost his life in Bangkok early on Sunday morning, after picking a fight with the wrong person. The 46-year-old was reportedly shouting at hotel staff, and then attacked a 39-year-old Italian guest getting into the elevator unprovoked. That Italian man was reportedly an MMA fighter, who put him in a chokehold, to the point that the American lost his life. While the man claims he was acting in self defense, he now potentially faces manslaughter charges.

It’s really sad how people act sometimes. We only have one life to live, and how unfortunate to cut your life short so unnecessarily.

#6008. What Are The World’s Tallest & Highest Hotels? The Answer Is Tricky…

There’s something I really love about staying in a hotel room on a really high floor, where you’re so high up that you almost feel like you’re in an airplane. So, what are the tallest and highest hotels in the world? I want to talk about that in this post, and also discuss why the answer isn’t that straightforward.

The question of which hotel is the tallest and highest isn’t as straightforward as you might assume. And even once we do define it, there’s the question of the extent to which the answer is actually useful. First let’s cover the distinction between the tallest hotel and the highest hotel.

Generally speaking, the tallest hotel would be defined as the tallest building where a large percent of the structure is made up of the hotel. Most commonly, I see people suggest that this would include situations where at least 80% of the building is the hotel.

This is different than the highest hotel, which would be the hotel that is highest above the ground, even if it only takes up a small percentage of a mixed-use building, where there might be apartments, residences, etc.

In other words, a 50-story building that consists exclusively of a hotel would fall into the former category, while a 110-story building where the top 10 floors are a hotel would fall into the latter category.

With that out of the way, let’s talk about the properties that are remarkable in these categories…

First, let’s cover some of the world’s tallest hotels. We’ll define this as hotels where at least 80% of the building consists of the hotel facility.

Let me of course mention one downside of very tall standalone hotels — you could end up being on a very low floor. After all, if a high-rise consists exclusively (or almost exclusively) of hotel facilities, some people will end up on very low floors. The other downside, of course, is that these hotels are necessarily huge. If you prefer boutique hotels, you won’t find any on this list.

Currently, the tallest hotel in the world is Ciel Tower Dubai. The 1,042-room hotel opened in 2024, rises to a height of 1,227 feet (374 meters), and has 82 floors.

To go over the list of the top five tallest hotels in the world:

As you can see, it’s interesting (but perhaps not surprising) that all four of the world’s tallest hotels are in Dubai.

The Conrad Shanghai, meanwhile, is located in the Shimao International Plaza, and this is the perfect example of how it’s tough to define what is technically the tallest. While the building it’s in rises to such a high height, roughly 25% of that height is the spire. So technically it’s a very tall building, but the usable space isn’t as high as you’d assume.

If you ask me, the world’s highest hotels are much more interesting than the world’s tallest hotels. That’s because the world’s highest hotels typically take up the top floors of some gravity-defying skyscrapers, and therefore, they can also be boutique properties.

When defining the world’s tallest hotels, there are some general challenges:

Because of the above, there are some minor disagreements as to which hotel wins the title, but I’ll share my take (while acknowledging that I don’t have the ability to scale buildings with a measuring tape).

Currently, the highest hotel is the Rosewood Guangzhou. The 251-room hotel opened in 2019, and it’s located at the top of the CTF Finance Centre Guangzhou, which reaches a height of 1,739 feet (530 meters).

To go over the list of the top five highest hotels in the world:

As you can see, those last two properties are kind of hard to judge, and particularly J Hotel Shanghai is tricky, given that the property is split between different parts of the building.

As the inverse of the above, I should mention that the Armani Hotel Dubai is located within the Burj Khalifa, which is the world’s tallest building. However, it’s located at the very bottom of the building, so that’s hardly that useful, for these purposes, since the hotel only goes as high as 39 floors.

Lastly, in the interest of being thorough, if we’re going to define a hotel as being “highest” based on the altitude above sea level, then we’d of course end up with a completely different list. Hotel Tayka del Desierto is located near the Salar de Uyuni salt flats in Bolivia. It’s at an altitude of 14,800 feet (4,500 meters), so it’s generally considered to be the highest up hotel in the world.

I suppose depending on how we want to define “hotel,” there would probably be some simple guest houses at Everest Base Camp that go even higher, but I don’t think that’s within the spirit of what I’m trying to cover here.

If you ask me, it’s always fun to stay in a hotel room that’s really high up. There’s an important distinction between the tallest hotels and the highest hotels, though sometimes, the exact rankings are a bit blurred.

While I’ve long been interested in this, I enjoyed researching this a bit more closely, and actually having a (sort of) definitive list. Ciel Tower Dubai is the world’s tallest hotel, while the Rosewood Guangzhou is the world’s highest hotel (unless you want to consider the 120th floor of the J Hotel Shanghai separately from the rest of the property).

Have you stayed at any of the world’s tallest or highest hotels? Does it even hold any appeal to you?

I enjoyed staying in the Signiel Seoul. Very quiet and surprisingly stable for the vertiginous height.

i have stayed at the gevora in dubai once and really can't recommend it. i think it's an old apartment building that was converted into a hotel and needs refurbishment. also, you gonna spend a lot of time in the elevators / waiting for them.

@jmd001 same here, the view matters more than the floor number. Park Hyatt KL is a good example, way up in Merdeka 118 with the whole skyline and the Petronas Towers in the distance. FWIW free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from dozens of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since inventory and rates differ by country. Then ask for a high floor facing the city when you book

Having to take multiple elevators to get to the room is just not appealing to me. I”m happier in regular height hotel.

I used to request high floors specifically, but funnily over the years, it's something I don't really care about too much anymore. The main advantage of high floors in big cities to me is that it's quieter, with less road noise. However, I generally dislike sky lobbies, especially if I have to take multiple elevators to get to my room. In some cities, it can be nice for the views, but often it's more of an inconvenience to me. Plus, it just feels more personal and (yes) "grounded" to be in a lowrise that's not part of some megacomplex. It's something I've come to appreciate more over the years.
