#5994. Southwest Airlines Plus Card Review: Modest Benefits For A Low Annual Fee

Southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

In my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card

Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:

Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most important factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

The Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

In terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

$99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:

Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

It’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

The Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

The Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

Southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

Another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

Each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

On your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

The Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

The Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

You’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up quickly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

If your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:

So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

If you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:

The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

The Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee. It’s not the most valuable Southwest credit card in the lineup, but its benefits and strong welcome bonus make it a good option at this price point.

If you want to learn more about the Southwest Plus Card, follow this link.

#5993. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#5992. Delta Is My Preferred Airline Of The “Big Three” US Carriers (Hear Me Out)

I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

Starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

Stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an issue using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

As such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to New York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

Neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

As a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

My experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this…

I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?

#5991. When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices…

Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

In most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

However, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

Broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is currently in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

It’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

Of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:

That being said, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

The above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:

On US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes issue with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

All airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no issues with using them for service.

Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

#5990. I sailed on Royal Caribbean's Legend of the Seas. Here are 5 things that surprised me

As one of the world's largest cruise ships, Royal Caribbean's Legend of the Seas promises no shortage of things to see, do and eat. With an expansive lineup of dining and entertainment venues, pools and activities, there's enough onboard to fill an entire vacation without ever stepping off the ship.

But as someone without extensive cruising experience, I boarded the ship with a few preconceived notions about what the rooms, crowds and restaurants would be like.

After sailing on the ship's inaugural voyage, however, I found myself pleasantly surprised by several aspects of the experience. Here are five things I didn't expect.

With thousands of passengers on board, I expected finding a place to lounge by the pool, grab a drink or simply sit and relax to be a bit of a challenge. After all, even the largest cruise ship in the world has a finite amount of space.

Given that the ship's double-occupancy capacity is 5,610, I was surprised by how rarely I felt surrounded by crowds.

I was traveling with a friend, and we could almost always find available lounge chairs; we rarely encountered long lines at restaurants, bars or other public areas. Elevators were easy to navigate, and I never felt like I was constantly waiting behind a crowd of other passengers.

There were a few exceptions. Some of the pools got busy, and popular performances and events filled up quickly, so planning ahead was important if I wanted to see something specific. But even during popular moments, like the rooftop deck fireworks display, there was enough room to enjoy the show without feeling packed in.

The same was true during our visit to Perfect Day at CocoCay, Royal Caribbean's private island in the Bahamas. We spent time at South Beach and Cove Beach, where there were plenty of open spots to settle in and enjoy a peaceful vibe.

For a ship carrying so many passengers — up to 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity — I was surprised by how easy it was to find a little breathing room.

Related: The ultimate guide to Royal Caribbean cruise ships and itineraries

Cruise lines aren't shy about advertising their entertainment, but I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from the actual productions. I figured there would be plenty of activities to keep passengers occupied, but I didn't anticipate the caliber of performances I saw onboard.

The AquaTheater show was one of the highlights of my sailing. The production featured acrobatics, high dives and aerial stunts that had the audience audibly gasping throughout the show.

The ice skating production Fusion was another standout. The performers were incredibly talented, and the show was engaging from beginning to end. There was also a full production of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” that I unfortunately didn't have time to see.

Beyond the major productions, there was plenty of entertainment to stumble upon throughout the ship. The live music was consistently good, and we happened upon a silent disco where passengers of all ages were dancing while listening to music through their own headphones.

We also participated in an onboard escape room, which was just as thoughtfully designed and challenging as some of the escape rooms I've experienced on land.

I went into the sailing thinking of entertainment as something to do between meals and pool time. Instead, it became one of the reasons I was excited to explore the ship.

Related: The 7 classes of Royal Caribbean cruise ships, explained

I knew Legend of the Seas would have plenty of dining options, from casual restaurants to more upscale specialty dining. But I wasn't expecting one of my favorite experiences of the entire sailing to be an eight-course tasting menu at the Hollywoodland Supper Club.

The experience felt completely removed from the typical cruise-ship dining environment. The restaurant's glamorous old Hollywood decor, live musical quartet and immersive atmosphere made dinner feel like an evening out in its own right.

The eight-course menu was thoughtfully presented, with each dish accompanied by a corresponding cocktail. Our servers were incredibly knowledgeable about the food and drinks, and there were little surprises throughout the meal, including an amuse-bouche to start and an unexpected dessert at the end.

Some highlights included blinis with caviar and goat cheese, which came paired with what the restaurant called a Sunset Martini, and the wagyu filet, which was paired with the club’s version of an Old Fashioned. Even the palate cleanser — a vodka-infused sorbet presented theatrically under a smoky glass top — was well thought out and delicious.

It was a three-hour dining experience with enough time to enjoy each course, discuss all the flavors with my tablemates, enjoy the live music (which included songs that coincided with each course) and get excited about what was coming next in the story. For a few hours, I almost forgot I was eating aboard a cruise ship.

I assumed this ship would have plenty of casual, approachable, kid-friendly dining options (which it did), but this experience made me realize there are also opportunities for a more sophisticated night out onboard.

With so many restaurants, bars, pools, entertainment venues and distinct neighborhoods, I assumed it would take me a while to get my bearings on Legend of the Seas. But the ship's size never felt overwhelming, and I found it surprisingly easy to navigate. Clear signage made it simple to find my way between venues, elevator displays helped me figure out where I needed to go, and crew members were always nearby if I had a question.

That ease extended beyond the ship itself. The Wi-Fi connection was strong enough that I could research the different beaches and amenities at Perfect Day at CocoCay before we arrived, making it easy to plan how I wanted to spend my day. Once ashore, complimentary trams made it simple to get between different areas of the island without having to walk everywhere.

For a ship with so much happening at once, I appreciated how little effort it took to get where I wanted to go and make the most of my time.

Related: The best Royal Caribbean cruise ship for every type of traveler

Before this sailing, I had always pictured cruise ship cabins as fairly cramped spaces with just enough room for a bed and a small bathroom. I expected to spend most of my time out exploring the ship and very little time actually enjoying my room.

My cabin on Legend of the Seas changed that perception.

I stayed in a Spacious Infinite Ocean View Balcony Room, which had a large bed, a couch and a sitting area by the floor-to-ceiling window. There wasn't a true balcony, but the sitting area and full floor-to-ceiling window gave a balcony-like feel. Guests in these rooms can open and close the windows using a button on the side of the window.

There was a surprising amount of storage available in the room. Between the full closet, dresser drawers and bathroom shelves, there was plenty of room to unpack and keep everything organized rather than living out of a suitcase. There was also enough space for two people to get ready without constantly maneuvering around each other.

Of course, a cruise ship cabin isn't going to offer the same square footage as a traditional hotel room. But I was impressed by how thoughtfully the space was laid out and how comfortable it felt for two people.

#5988. Where To Spot The Air France Airbus A318 Before It Finally Retires

Air France's Airbus A318 was due to disappear from scheduled passenger service on November 8, but its retirement has been pushed back to March 27, 2027. The airline's remaining aircraft are still operating from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), with Marseille (MRS), Toulouse (TLS), Bordeaux (BOD), Nice (NCE), Milan Linate (LIN), and Lyon (LYS) offering some of the most frequent opportunities to catch the type.

Using data from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker, we analyzed 423 A318 flights between October 12 and November 8. The four aircraft visited 30 airports during those four weeks. One stopped appearing after October 20, although it has since returned to service. Their movements provide a useful indication of where and when to look, particularly for anyone planning a visit to Paris in the coming months.

The smallest member of the Airbus A320 family has already received several extensions to its service life with Air France. Last summer, the carrier extended planned A318 operations from November 8, 2026, until March 27, 2027. The revised timetable covers domestic French routes and a selection of intra-European destinations, with all the scheduled services operating through CDG.

However, March 27 is the final date currently shown in the published schedule rather than a confirmed farewell flight. Aircraft assignments can also change independently of the route timetable, meaning the presence of an A318 in a booking system does not guarantee that passengers will actually travel on one. For spotters, recent movements are consequently more useful than relying entirely on flights advertised several months ahead.

Air France has continued replacing its smaller A320-family aircraft with the Airbus A220-300. On November 6, the airline received its 60th A220, registered F-HOZJ, which subsequently entered passenger service on November 9. The new aircraft seats 148 passengers, compared with 131 on the A318, and is now used across much of the airline's European network. Nevertheless, the four remaining A318s continue to appear in daily operations.

The busiest A318 route during our four-week analysis was between CDG and Marseille Provence Airport (MRS), with 69 recorded flights in both directions. Of these, 35 departed Paris and 34 returned from Marseille. Toulouse-Blagnac Airport (TLS) came second with 47 flights, followed by Bordeaux–Mérignac Airport (BOD) with 42. Together, these three domestic connections accounted for 158 flights, or more than a third of the total activity recorded.

Nice Côte d'Azur Airport (NCE) was the fourth most frequently visited destination, with 28 flights. The leading international route was Milan Linate Airport (LIN), with 22, while Lyon–Saint Exupéry Airport (LYS) recorded 20. These six routes accounted for 228 of the 423 flights, making them the most useful starting points for anyone trying to photograph the aircraft away from CDG. The figures reflect actual recorded movements, not the number of A318 flights scheduled in the months ahead.

Marseille is particularly interesting because the A318 appeared on several different rotations rather than being restricted to a single flight number. AF7344 was recorded ten times from Paris during the analysis, while AF7336 appeared on eight departures. The late-evening AF7344 also operated with F-GUGP on November 21, according to subsequent flight history.

Airbus's whale-shaped jet keeps its operation moving across Europe and beyond.

Despite their small number, the A318s were used across a geographically diverse network. We identified 30 different airports in 12 countries between October 12 and November 8, including CDG itself. France accounted for nine of these airports, while the aircraft also visited five in Italy, four in Spain, and two in Portugal. Outside these markets, the tracking data included destinations such as Amsterdam (AMS), Copenhagen (CPH), Warsaw (WAW), Munich (MUC), Prague (PRG), and Bergen (BGO).

The aircraft were not limited to routes typically associated with the French domestic network. Recorded international flights include Paris to Casablanca Mohammed V International Airport (CMN), Málaga (AGP), and Ibiza Airport (IBZ). Bergen Airport (BGO) also appeared in the data, although each of these destinations was served far less frequently than the main domestic routes. A route appearing once or twice in four weeks should not be interpreted as a dependable spotting opportunity.

Unsurprisingly, of the 423 recorded flights, 422 either departed from or arrived at CDG. The exception was a one-off flight between Bologna (BLQ) and Venice (VCE) on November 6. The French hub airport therefore remains the most obvious location for seeing one without having to predict its next destination, although the timing of a visit makes a substantial difference.

This is the detour the world's longest Airbus A321XLR flight takes every day.

As each of the active A318s generally completes around five flights on a flying day, the aircraft make repeated appearances at CDG throughout the day. Our tracking data contains 213 departures from the airport during the 28-day period, equivalent to an average of approximately eight daily departures across the remaining fleet. These were not evenly distributed across the day, however, and several periods offered considerably more activity than others.

The most useful morning window was between 7:00 AM and 8:59 AM local time, when 49 A318 departures were recorded. Another 44 departures took place between noon and 1:59 PM, while 49 occurred between 6:00 PM and 9:59 PM. The later flights are less useful for photography during the winter months, although they provide additional opportunities for anyone primarily interested in watching or flying the aircraft.

Particularly at CDG, it is worth following the registration rather than concentrating on just one scheduled departure. An A318 arriving from Bordeaux, Marseille, or Milan may continue to an entirely different destination after its turnaround. Watching the aircraft's inbound sector can therefore help establish whether the same airframe is likely to operate the next flight, rather than waiting for a single flight number that may be assigned another type.

We tracked hundreds of flights in 2 weeks, revealing the busiest diversion airports, major disruption waves and 3 extraordinary detours in the world

Four registrations appear in the four-week dataset: F-GUGM, F-GUGN, F-GUGO, and F-GUGP. The busiest was F-GUGM, which completed 146 flights and was recorded on all 28 days. F-GUGO operated 129 flights across 26 days, while F-GUGN recorded 102 flights across 21 days after first appearing on October 19. On days when they flew, each aircraft generally operated around five sectors, although individual daily totals varied.

F-GUGP followed a different pattern as the aircraft completed 46 flights during the first nine days of the period, with its final recorded departure on October 20, when it flew from CDG to Casablanca. It did not appear again in our data through November 8. Consequently, the four-week figures primarily reflect the activity of three aircraft during the second half of the period, rather than a consistently deployed four-aircraft fleet.

More recent data shows F-GUGP operating AF7344 from CDG to Marseille on November 21, departing at 8:15 PM and landing at 9:21 PM. Its return to flying demonstrates why a list of active registrations needs to be checked against current movements, particularly as the retirement date approaches.

The A318's wider route network may contain many possible destinations, but the availability of the actual aircraft will determine which services operate as planned. With only four registrations to follow, a single aircraft being unavailable can affect a sizeable proportion of the type's daily flying. That is also why an A318 shown against a route weeks in advance is not necessarily the aircraft that will turn up on departure day.

The easiest way to identify an A318 currently flying is to open the Simple Flying Live Flight Tracker and search for the aircraft type or one of the four registrations. F-GUGM, F-GUGN, F-GUGO, and F-GUGP provide a much narrower starting point than following every Air France flight from Paris. Filtering the map around CDG then makes it possible to see which aircraft are airborne and where they are heading.

To find out where Air France's last A318s will fly, the most useful approach is to check the recent history of the individual aircraft and then compare it with the airline's upcoming flights. The four-week data suggests beginning with Marseille, Toulouse, and Bordeaux, before considering Nice, Milan Linate, or Lyon. However, the registration assigned on the day is more important than how often a particular route appears in October or early November.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The tracker also allows you to follow the aircraft without traveling to France, while registration-level histories reveal patterns that published schedules miss. When the final A318 flights take place, the same historical data should provide the most reliable record of which aircraft operated the last passenger service, rather than relying on the timetable alone.

#5987. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Here’s every promotion on purchased IHG Rewards Points we’ve tracked since January 2026, with the cost per point for each, so you can see how the current deal stacks up.

Is this a good deal? At 0.54 cents per point, the current promotion is 50% below the standard price. That matches the best deal we’ve tracked.

Cost per point at the largest purchase tier, including the 7.5% tax. Lower is better.

Every IHG Rewards Club buy points promotion since January 2026

*Cost per point is for the largest purchase tier and includes the 7.5% tax.

Between 12:01 AM ET on November 23 and 11:59PM ET on December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that). Furthermore, the purchase of points is non-refundable.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 300,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 600,000 points at a cost of $3,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 300,000 points, pre-bonus.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

#5986. Chase Freedom Unlimited Review: No Annual Fee & 1.5x Points Everywhere

The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®

Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:

Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited currently has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

On the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

It’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

These intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

Eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

There’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized users to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

However, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:

With one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:

This can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

One thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:

That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

For a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for new purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

With Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash plan after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

DoorDash DashPass gets you $0 delivery fees and lower service fees on eligible orders through both the DoorDash and Caviar delivery platforms. You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is currently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

If you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

I’d also like to look a bit more closely at the best strategy to take with the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have. That’s because not only can you combine the benefits of the two cards, but this greatly increases the value you get from your Freedom Unlimited points.

For example, if you have the Sapphire Reserve and Freedom Unlimited:

There are currently two Chase Freedom products you can apply for — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and Chase Freedom Flex® Credit Card (learn more). Both cards have no annual fees, so what are the major differences between the cards?

The cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

Chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

Other than those differences, the two cards are very similar. I have both of these cards (yes, I have a lot of Chase credit cards).

The Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) is probably the closest competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, regardless of whether you’re looking to earn points or cash back.

The Citi Double Cash also has no annual fee and offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back after you pay for that purchase in the form of ThankYou points. So you’ll earn 2.0 cents back on the dollar, rather than 1.5. Furthermore, in conjunction with a card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) or Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), you can move points at the best possible ratio to travel partners.

Since I value Citi ThankYou and Chase Ultimate Rewards points roughly equally, this could also be an attractive card for everyday spending.

The reason some people may still prefer the Freedom Unlimited is because of the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem. On top of that, the Freedom Unlimited has bonus categories, which the Citi Double Cash doesn’t have.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, and it has a few pros and cons. The Capital One VentureOne has no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees, and offers a minimum of 1.25x miles per dollar spent.

Those miles can either be redeemed for one cent each toward a travel purchase, or they can be moved to Capital One’s airline and hotel transfer partners.

The downside of the VentureOne is that the rewards structure isn’t as lucrative, on the surface. The upside, though, is the lack of foreign transaction fees, and the ability to directly transfer points to airline and hotel partners, even without having another card.

So which card is better depends on whether you’re looking for a “one size fits all” no annual fee card, or want to use it as part of a larger strategy.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a key card to maximizing your overall Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, in conjunction with the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, and offers a minimum of 1.5x points per dollar spent. Let me make my advice as concise as possible here: if you have the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, then you absolutely should have the Freedom Unlimited, so you’re maximizing your return on everyday, non-bonused Chase spending.

Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®

#5985. American Airlines Drops Chicago Gate Lawsuit, But Doubles Down On Turf War With United

American Airlines is dropping its lawsuit against the City of Chicago and United Airlines over the controversial redistribution of gates at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). The decision follows an unsuccessful appeal last week, bringing the carrier's 18-month legal battle over the allocation of airport infrastructure toward a close.

However, American is arguably in a stronger competitive position at O'Hare than when it first launched its legal challenge. The airline has recovered gate space, significantly expanded its network, and announced further investments in its third-largest hub. Nevertheless, Reuters reports that United's continued dominance in Chicago presents a considerable obstacle to American's ambitions of rebuilding a profitable operation.

In a court filing dated November 20, as reported by View From The Wing, American requested that its entire complaint be dismissed with prejudice, meaning it would be unable to pursue the same claims again, including those for financial damages. Neither Chicago nor United opposes the motion, with each party bearing its own legal expenses under the proposed dismissal. American explained its decision in a statement to View From The Wing:

“We stand by our decision to advocate for a fair process, and today, we believe the best way to continue delivering on that commitment is to look ahead.”

The dispute originated in O'Hare's 2018 Airline Use and Lease Agreement (AULA), which allows gates to be redistributed according to airlines' flight activity. American argued that delays in delivering additional gates in Concourse L meant that a contractually agreed expansion period had not been fulfilled, precluding any redistribution until 2027. Unsurprisingly, the City of Chicago and United disagreed.

Chicago adopts a new lease agreement, allowing periodic gate redistribution based on airlines' shares of departures.

Delta's relocation to Terminal 5 triggers a protected expansion period. American's anticipated additional Concourse L gates remain unavailable.

At United's request, Chicago begins redistributing gate space based on 2024 flight activity.

American sues Chicago in federal court, seeking to prevent redistribution until April 2027.

Chicago finalizes the new allocations, with American losing four gates and United gaining five.

United joins the federal case, raising jurisdictional issues. American withdraws that case and files a state court complaint on July 16.

Following a seven-day hearing, the court denies American's request for an injunction to block the redistribution.

The revised gate allocations take effect, strengthening United's position at O'Hare. American appeals the denial of its preliminary injunction.

Chicago and United submit their formal responses to American's complaint.

Proceedings on the underlying complaint are suspended pending resolution of the appeal.

The appellate court upholds the injunction denial, citing the balance of harm to airlines, passengers and airport operations.

American moves to permanently dismiss its complaint, including its outstanding damages claims.

Sources: Illinois Appellate Court ruling, American's dismissal motion and Chicago Department of Aviation.

Notably, the appellate court did not definitively determine whether Chicago had breached its contractual obligations. Rather, it concluded that the potential disruption from reversing the redistribution outweighed the harm that American faced. The airline could have continued pursuing compensation, but its commercial circumstances at O'Hare have changed considerably since it filed the original complaint.

American's aggressive expansion at O'Hare has already yielded tangible results. In June, Chicago confirmed that American had earned additional gate space through its increased flight activity, reversing much of the previous year's losses. Separately, the carrier strengthened its position by paying $30 million to acquire the preferential-use leasehold rights for gates G8 and G10 from Spirit Airlines under its Chapter 11 proceedings.

United CEO Scott Kirby had previously vowed to prevent American from gaining further gates at United's expense, targeting 750 daily departures from Chicago. However, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) intervened over congestion concerns, forcing United to cut more than 100 daily departures. Reuters reports that those flight restrictions have subsequently been extended through October 2027, limiting United's ability to overwhelm American through additional frequencies.

*Net gate position reflects four gates lost, three regained, and two acquired

American's expansion has also strengthened Chicago's long-haul connectivity. The carrier launched flights to Naples and Honolulu last year, with nonstop service to Maui commencing on December 17. Furthermore, its return to Tokyo Narita in March next year will give American its 11th long-haul route from O'Hare, underscoring its ambitions to rebuild Chicago as an international gateway.

Despite American's progress, considerable financial and competitive challenges remain. United's faster post-pandemic recovery has enabled it to establish a substantial market share advantage. More concerningly, a Deutsche Bank analysis reported by Reuters in February highlighted the enormous disparity between the financial performance of the two airlines' respective Chicago operations.

United is also strengthening its customer proposition through its United Next fleet modernization program and the rollout of free Starlink connectivity, which is scheduled for fleetwide completion by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, O'Hare's infrastructure expansion will unlock significant additional growth opportunities, with 19 new gates in Concourse D in 2028 and a further 14 in Concourse E in 2030.

However, American is making substantial customer experience investments of its own. Its new Concourse L Admirals Club will open in 2027, doubling the existing lounge's footprint, while premium cabins are now available on every Chicago departure. Having successfully defended its ability to compete at O'Hare, American's next challenge will be translating its expanded presence and improved passenger experience into sustainable profitability.

#5984. Park Hyatt Dubai Reopening In 2027, After Full Renovation: First Look At New Rooms

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the new room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how big you want the property to be, to what you value most.

After all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:

To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

There are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Plan miles for Emirates first class.

Remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that says nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:

Park Hyatt Dubai is currently closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

As it currently stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

The hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the new room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

Leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things currently stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

The Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is currently undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a new beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful update since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the new rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?
