#5983. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#5982. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an update to reflect that.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-new cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico)

For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

Side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉

While details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#5980. Why The US Military Is Expanding A Remote Pacific Airport To Reduce Its Reliance On Guam

In October and November, I visited the Micronesian island countries of Palau and the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). The FSM consists of four states: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae. I visited Yap, whose airport is set to receive some major work by the United States to prepare it for war as part of the USAF's broader Agile Combat Employment (ACE) doctrine to disperse aircraft from Guam. Separately, US Navy personnel on the island informed me that there are plans to dredge the island's harbor to allow large warships to berth. Funding has not yet been approved.

When I visited, work on the airport had not yet started, and the US military footprint on the island was minimal. The hotel I stayed at houses around half the personnel (mostly US Navy) on the island for periods of six months. I arrived in Yap from Palau, where the minor airfield of Peleliu was closed because major construction work to expand the airport for ACE operations was underway. Here is what to know about the US's plans to expand Yap International Airport to relieve wartime strain on Andersen Air Force Base in Guam.

The knowledge that Yap Island's airport was soon to be transformed was surreal. The island is one of the remote islands in the Pacific and is difficult and expensive to reach. Adjacent to the international airport is an old Japanesee WWII airfield littered with aircraft destroyed by American bombing and lost to the jungle. I found around eight Japanese airplanes, some marked, some not marked. Here and there around the islands are the remains of lost US Vought F4U Corsairs and bombers.

Today, the island feels like a world away, but the USAF plans to improve the airports and airfields on the Second Island Chain as competition with China heats up. The echoes from WWII are clear. In 1944, the US island-hopped to Japan to project airpower over the Japanese home islands.

Now those same islands are needed to project airpower over the First Island Chain. The First Island Chain includes Taiwan, Japan's southern islands, and the Philippines. Following WWII, the US consolidated its airpower and military bases on Guam, while maintaining forward bases in Japan and Korea. The rise of China puts not only those forward bases at risk, but also Guam, which is now a prime target. Without Guam, or an effective alternative, the US's ability to project airpower over the region would diminish drastically.

The WWII US invasion of the island of Peleliu was one of the deadliest operations for the US Marines during the Pacific War. Fortunately for the native Yapese, the island was not invaded. Instead, it was intensively bombed, bypassed, and rendered irrelevant. Japanese forces remained on the island until the surrender. Most of their aircraft were destroyed in air campaigns.

The Japanese airfield is now abandoned and overgrown, but next to it, Yap International Airport operates. Yap Airport is a simple single-runway airport with a basic terminal building. The only scheduled passenger flights that use the airport are United Airlines and Pacific Missionary Aviation (PMA) United operates 737 MAX 8 flights from Guam twice weekly; this is the primary connection to the outside world. Outside of United's flights, Yap's terminal building is generally closed.

PMA operates passenger flights once a week (soon to be twice) from neighboring Palau using its two Super King Airs (seven to nine seats, depending on freight). PMA also operates flights to Yap's outlying islands as well as MEDEVAC and emergency services. I flew the PMA passenger flight from Palau to Yap, was invited on a flight to an outlying island (Ulithi), and flew out on United. PMA operates from its own private hangar and operates domestic flights from there. International (Palau) flights run through the main terminal.

Why the USAF is restoring ruins on the far flung island of Tinian.

Funding for Yap Airport's transformation appears in two main categories: civilian FAA Airport Improvement Program (AIP) grants and the Department of Defense/Air Force military construction and related funding. The Air Force's Fiscal Year 2025 Military Construction budget request included around $400 million for runway extension and related work. This is labeled "PDI: Runway Extension, Inc." in the documents. The first increment funding is $96 million.

A modest reduction appears in Fiscal 2027 documents with the explanatory note, "Program execution encountered delays and slipped from FY2025 to FY2026, funding reflects the one-time decrease after increase to support acquisition of land for an agreed upon defense site under appropriate international agreement required to complete the runway extension, parking apron, and taxiway construction at Yap International Airport, Wake Island."

The decrease is $31 million, but as the note includes Wake Island, it is unclear how much of this is relevant to Yap. The justification language for the funding emphasizes the need for a longer runway and facilities to support larger military aircraft for training, operations, contingency, and Agile Combat Employment. In the event of a high-end conflict with China, this likely means that Yap will be on China's list of strategic targets to be hit and neutralized.

The United States is currently upgrading numerous airports and airfields across the Second Island Chain as part of its ACE doctrine and preparations to counter China. As stated, one of the most significant programs currently underway is rehabilitating Palau's Peleliu airfield, while Angaur Airfield is already complete. On Guam, the USAF is expanding parking areas on its primary Andersen Air Force Base and rehabilitating its adjacent, formerly abandoned Northwest Field.

One of the biggest areas of effort is on the island of Tinian in the Northern Mariana Islands. There, the USAF is expanding and rehabilitating Tinian International Airport and the formerly abandoned North Field. Nearby, the island of Rota (home to fewer than 2,000 inhabitants) has also been an area of interest and increased military exercises. The civil airports on Palau, Saipan, and Guam also factor into US ACE planning, even if no work is being carried out to expand them.

Select Micronesian airports/airfields being expanded for ACE (per budget documents)

One important effort is Australia. Australia is not part of the Second Island Chain, and the relationship with Washington is very different from that of small Pacific islands. In Australia, effort is mostly focused on Australia's northern RAAF bases: Tindal, RAAF Darwin, and possibly RAAF Amberley. These are being prepped primarily for US strategic bomber use with associated aerial tankers.

Following WWII, the United States occupied the Japanese South Seas Mandate and formally took over administration as the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (TTPI). Eventually, the Trust Territory was broken up. The Northern Mariana Islands joined the United States as a commonwealth, while Palau, the FSM, and the Marshall Islands became independent nations with full United Nations membership.

However, sovereignty for these islands is nuanced. As part of the process, the newly independent states signed the Compacts of Free Association with the United States. Of interest to this article is that the United States retained responsibility for the defense of the islands. In practical terms, this gives the US military the benefits of basing in US territories without the islands actually being US territories.

The FSM government states, "Under the Compact, the United States provides financial assistance, defends the FSM’s territorial integrity, and allows FSM citizens unrestricted travel to the U.S. In return, the FSM grants the United States exclusive access to its land and waterways for strategic purposes." The Compact grants the United States "full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters," although in practice, the US extensively collaborates with the government rather than dictates.

Visiting Yap today, it is surreal to feel so isolated and yet also see the island reprising its role as potentially returning to the frontline of a major Pacific competition. In the years ahead, the airport may start to see the deployment of US tankers and F-35 fighter jets just hundreds of feet (meters) away from the rusting hulks of Japanese Zeros and American Corsairs rotting in the jungle.

In WWII, the US Navy drew up a plan to invade Yap, but this was scrapped in favor of bombarding it and bypassing it. China’s primary counter to ACE is the continued expansion of the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force (PLARF) and supporting systems, including large inventories of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hypersonic missiles. These are intended to hold US airfields at risk across the First and Second Island Chains.

The US is aware of this. Increasingly, the US Air Force, Marines, and Navy are focusing on increasing the range of next-generation fighter jets (e.g., F-47 and F/A-XX). Logistics and assault requirements increasingly focus on being runway-independent, with the US Army's incoming MV-75 tiltrotor being an example. The Marines, in particular, are investing in a range of runway-independent and sea-skimming drone options for the 'last mile' of resupply and MEDEVAC.

#5979. New York JFK Terminal 6 Is Almost Open: Airlines & Lounges Moving In

New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:

The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

All things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:

There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

Now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the new lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s new lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

Are you excited for the new JFK Terminal 6?

#5978. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#5977. Capital One Venture Card Bonus: 75K Miles + $300 Credit Welcome Offer (Last Chance)

At the moment, the $95 annual fee Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is offering a phenomenal limited time welcome bonus, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d like to provide an update that this is the last chance to pick up the card with this offer, as it’s expected to be pulled soon.

Not only is this among the best offers we’ve seen on the card, but this is also a reasonably priced travel rewards card that offers long term value, especially for everyday spending.

Link: Learn more about the Capital One Venture Card

The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

For context, Capital One miles can be redeemed for a minimum of one cent each, meaning the 75,000 miles will get you at least $750 in value. However, I value the miles at 1.7 cents each based on my latest analysis (see my methodology here), thanks to the value you can get by transferring the miles to travel partners. That means that to me, the 75,000 miles are worth $1,275.

There are lots of great ways to redeem Capital One miles, as they can be transferred to Capital One’s roughly 20 airline and hotel partners. That’s my preferred use of them, as you can get some amazing travel experiences this way.

Partners include programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and more. These are all programs that allow you to really maximize your points and get outsized value. Just to give a couple of examples of Capital One mileage redemption opportunities:

That doesn’t include the value of the $300 Capital One Travel credit, which posts upon account approval (rather than upon completing minimum spending). The idea is that this can be used for a hotel or vacation rental booking through Capital One Travel in your first cardmember year (in the first 12 months), and it’s valid across one or multiple stays. In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer. Quite to the contrary, when this limited time offer gets pulled, it’ll almost certainly be worse.

For context, below is a history of the publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the Capital One Venture in recent years.

As you can see, we’ve never seen a publicly available welcome offer of over 75,000 miles, in terms of the mileage component. We have in the past seen $250 travel credits offered along with the miles, and this time around the travel credit is bigger. So offers really don’t get better than this on the card.

When you look at the bonus terms on the Capital One Venture Card, you’ll find the following language:

You are not eligible for this product if you have received a new cardmember bonus for the Capital One Venture card or the Capital One Venture X card in the past 48 months.

As you can see, the card follows a 48-month rule, so you’re not eligible for the welcome bonus on this card if you’ve received a new cardmember bonus on this exact card or on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) in the past 48 months.

Other than that, eligibility is unrelated to having any other credit card, and Capital One doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for cards.

The Capital One Venture Card has a reasonable $95 annual fee, and offers a variety of perks beyond the excellent welcome bonus:

While the Capital One Venture Card is awesome, how does it compare to the Capital One Venture X Card, which is Capital One’s ultra premium credit card? The Venture X has a $395 annual fee, so the fee is significantly higher, but it also offers several great perks that should more than justify the annual fee. Among other things, the Venture X offers:

So when it comes to the Capital One Venture vs. Venture X, personally I think the Venture X is an even better value than the Venture. However, I know some people just want to avoid higher annual fee cards in general, so for those people, the Venture could be a better option.

The limited time Capital One Venture Card bonus currently offers 75,000 Capital One miles plus a $300 Capital One Travel credit upon completing minimum spending. This Capital One Venture bonus is significantly better than usual, so if you’re eligible for the card based on the 48-month bonus rule, I’d absolutely recommend applying. This is the last chance, as the offer is expected to be pulled soon.

Anyone plan to pick up the Capital One Venture Card with this great bonus?

#5976. US Army Moves To Restart Washington DC Helicopter Training Flights 2 Years After Deadly Crash

The US Army is moving to resume helicopter training flights in airspace near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) as soon as the week of December 6, according to a recent report by Politico. That timeline comes less than two years after the January 29, 2025 midair collision between an Army Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk and a PSA Airlines regional jet operating as American Airlines Flight 5342 over the Potomac River, a disaster that killed all 67 people aboard both aircraft.

Training operations in the corridor were halted in May 2025 after an Army Black Hawk came too close to Reagan National and forced approaching commercial airliners to abort landings. Resuming training requires Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval, and the service had not yet filed a formal request with regulators even as military officials briefed congressional staff on their plans.

Existing FAA regulations explicitly exclude routine training from essential flight categories in the restricted zone around Reagan National. Under interim final rule 2026-01226, which took effect on January 23, 2026, and permanently closed Helicopter Route 4 between Hains Point and the Wilson Bridge, only rare essential flights may enter designated airspace up to 1,500 feet (457 meters) mean sea level. Those narrow exceptions cover lifesaving medical missions, active law enforcement responses to ongoing crimes, national defense or counterintelligence operations, continuity of government, and transport of the President or Vice President.

The rule specifies that proficiency evaluations, routine training, and non-essential personnel transport do not qualify as essential operations. Because the regulation bars routine training inside the designated Potomac zone, military leaders would need either a formal regulatory modification or an approved authorization pathway before standard pilot currency missions resume. FAA officials opened public comment on the interim rule through February 23, 2026, and indicated a final rule would follow after reviewing submissions, eliminated visual separation within five nautical miles (9.3 km) of the airport, increased staffing and oversight, and required air traffic controllers to manage commercial runway use when essential vertical-lift aircraft enter restricted airspace.

Investigations by the National Transportation Safety Board and the Army traced the January 2025 collision to overlapping operational, technical, and airspace vulnerabilities rather than a single error. National Transportation Safety Board findings and reporting by Task & Purpose highlighted tight vertical margins near low-altitude river routes, radio frequency congestion, altimeter instrumentation discrepancies, and bright urban lighting that complicated visual detection at night.

Investigators also noted that radio transmissions that might have helped crews confirm visual separation were missed or complicated by overlapping traffic. The National Transportation Safety Board issued 50 safety recommendations, including eight directed at the Army, and concluded that an Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast system could have alerted the airliner crew 59 seconds before impact. In response, the Army conducted fleet inspections, tested altimeters across Black Hawk variants, and reviewed crew separation procedures. These technical and procedural reviews reflect a broader effort to pair airframe checks with stricter altitude discipline across congested metropolitan corridors.

It is a very dangerous place for both commercial and non-commercial aircraft alike.

Pushback from aviation labor unions and pending legislation on Capitol Hill complicate the Army's push for a December restart. Association of Flight Attendants president Sara Nelson condemned plans to bring military training back near Reagan National so soon after the fatal crash.

Meanwhile, lawmakers remain divided over final statutory mandates governing shared airspace and traffic-alerting equipment. According to The Washington Sun and Senate Commerce Committee reporting, the Rotor Operations Transparency and Oversight Reform Act passed the Senate unanimously in December 2025 but stalled in the House, though leaders announced an agreement in principle in mid-November 2026 on a framework to reconcile competing bills before the end of the year. Negotiations involving the House Armed Services Committee remain central to settling how military helicopters and fixed-wing planes share crowded corridors, while commuters and airlines watch whether flight delays or runway adjustments could return. While Senators Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell push to finish the legislation, unresolved details over military aircraft equipment requirements continue to draw scrutiny from safety advocates and families of the victims.

#5975. Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s new Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:

It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time…

What do you make of Delta’s plans to fly to Singapore?

Between Black Friday deals, gifts for family and friends and all the other expenses that come with the holiday season, it's easy for spending to add up.

But with the right credit card, it can also be one of the most rewarding times of the year.

Whether you're shopping online or in-store, choosing a card that aligns with your spending habits can help you earn valuable points, miles or cash back on your purchases. Some cards also offer valuable perks, like purchase protection, that can come in handy during the holiday season.

Here are our picks for the best credit cards for holiday shopping in 2026.

The information for the Prime Visa has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards is a great option for those who want to earn flexible rewards without worrying about different spending category bonuses. The Venture Rewards earns 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases — ensuring that you earn bonus miles no matter if you’re buying stocking stuffers or perusing Cyber Monday deals.

There’s also flexibility in how you redeem those miles you earn. You can use your miles to “pay” yourself back for travel booked in the past 90 days. Or, you can transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel loyalty programs to book new travel. You can also redeem miles for gift cards or statement credits for eligible purchases.

The is a great option for earning bonus rewards year-round, thanks to its rotating quarterly categories.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, cardholders can earn 5% cash back on grocery store purchases and American Red Cross donations, plus an elevated 7% cash back on dining purchases. That could come in handy if you're stocking up for holiday gatherings or dining out with family and friends.

These bonus rates apply to up to $1,500 in combined purchases across the quarterly categories through Dec. 31, after which you'll earn 1% back. You must activate the categories by Dec. 14 to qualify.

While 5% cash back is appealing on its own, the Freedom Flex can be even more valuable when paired with a Chase card that earns transferable Ultimate Rewards points, such as the (see rates and fees), or the (see rates and fees).

By combining your rewards, you can transfer points to airline and hotel partners, including United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt, potentially getting more value from your holiday spending. Note that the Sapphire Preferred offers a 4:3 transfer ratio for World of Hyatt.

To learn more, read our full review of the Freedom Flex.

If you’re a regular Amazon shopper, the Prime Visa is the card for you, with no annual fee (though it requires an Amazon Prime membership).

With Black Friday and Cyber Monday coming, you want a card that gives you the biggest bang for your holiday shopping buck. The Prime Visa offers unlimited 5% on Amazon, Whole Foods and Chase Travel, 2% on restaurants, gas stations and local transit and commuting and 1% on all other purchases. Additionally, earn 10% or more on a rotating selection of items and categories on Amazon.com.

If you don’t have the card already, new applicants will instantly get a $150 Amazon gift card upon approval, exclusively for Prime members.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Prime Visa.

Without question, the is one of the best cards for foodies. The card offers an impressive 4 points per dollar spent at U.S. supermarkets (up to $25,000 spent per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent) and restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

While the earning rate for nonbonus purchases yields 1 point per dollar spent, you may want to consider paying with the Amex Gold this holiday season for its strong purchase protection policy. Eligible items are covered for up to $10,000 in theft, damage, or loss within the first 90 days of purchase (up to $50,000 per calendar year).*

That’s considerable, especially if you buy big-ticket items like electronics or furniture.

The Amex Gold also comes with extended warranty protection, which prolongs a U.S. manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of five years or less.*

You’ll never know when you need to rely on these protections, but they can be quite valuable and may be worth sacrificing the bonus points you’d earn from the other cards on this list, even after factoring in the $325 annual fee.

*Eligibility and benefit levels vary by card. Terms, conditions, and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Gold.

If you have the ability to park a significant amount of your investments and savings at Bank of America or Merrill, the is a great option for holiday purchases.

While the card comes with reasonable (though not earth-shattering) earning rates of 2 points per dollar spent on travel and dining and 1.5 points per dollar spent on all purchases (which can be redeemed at the rate of 1 cent per point), the real value of this card comes when you can make it to either the Preferred Honors or Premier award tiers in the BofA Rewards™ program.

By doing so, the everyday earning rate on this card can jump all the way up to roughly 2.6 points for every dollar spent, making it a terrific choice for holiday gifts.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Premium Rewards.

The final card on our list earns a spot in part for its simplicity. The offers a flat 1% back on every purchase plus another 1% back as you pay your bill (up to a 2% total return).

While this return rate on everyday purchases doesn’t compare to the potential returns highlighted above, this is automatic; it results in cold, hard cash in your account. For many shoppers, a no-annual-fee card like this fits the bill.

To learn more, read our full review of the Double Cash.

Holiday spending can do more than check gifts off your list — it can also help you reach big credit card goals. If you’ve recently opened a new card, consider putting your holiday purchases toward the minimum spending requirement to earn a valuable welcome bonus. Just be sure to budget responsibly and pay off your balance in full as often as you can.

If you already have multiple cards, check whether any offer calendar-year spending bonuses or perks that reset soon. Concentrating your purchases on one card could help you unlock statement credits, free nights or elite status before the year ends.

Another easy way to earn extra rewards is through online shopping portals. These portals let you earn additional points, miles or cash back just by clicking through before you buy (no special credit card required).

To find the best offer, use CashBack Monitor, which compares earning rates across dozens of portals for the same retailer. You can also install your preferred portal’s browser extension, so you’ll never miss out on bonus rewards during checkout.

Focus on cards that match your shopping habits, whether that means flat-rate cash back, bonus rewards on popular retailers or flexible travel points you can redeem later.

Pair your card with online shopping portals and seasonal category bonuses to earn even more rewards on every purchase. And if you’re opening a new card, use your holiday spending to hit minimum spend requirements and unlock valuable welcome offers.

With a little planning, your holiday shopping can turn into a rewards windfall, from extra points and cash back to future flights, hotel stays or statement credits, making this season both festive and rewarding.

#5971. Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Points With 80% Bonus (1.1 Cents Each): Worth It?

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is currently offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points. Through December 31, 2026, Flying Club members can purchase points with up to an 80% bonus, which is potentially an opportunity to buy points for under 1.1 cents each. Suffice it to say that this could be a very attractive deal.

Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus

Between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points. Virgin Atlantic is offering a tiered bonus of up to 80%, as follows:

Note that the purchase of Virgin Atlantic points is non-refundable, and purchasing points doesn’t count toward Flying Club elite status. Points will be credited to accounts within 24 hours, though they typically post faster than that, and almost instantly.

The cost to purchase Virgin Atlantic points varies based on where your account is registered:

The pricing is much better for those with accounts registered in the UK rather than the US. Assuming you’re eligible for an 80% bonus:

So as you can see, in the United States you can potentially pay 1.39 cents per point, while in the UK you can potentially pay 1.09 cents per point.

It’s interesting how much Virgin Atlantic penalizes those in the United States when it comes to buying points. Then again, when it comes to overall points earning opportunities, we can’t really complain in the United States, given the amazing credit card offers we have.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ordinarily lets members purchase up to 200,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been doubled, to 400,000 points.

When Virgin Atlantic Flying Club offers a promotion on purchased points, the best version of the offer is almost always for a 70% bonus. As you can tell, this offer is even better than those, as this is truly a best-ever offer. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Flying Club program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Flying Club points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

Nowadays Virgin Atlantic has dynamic award pricing for its own flights, and for those with flexibility who want the best deal, this can make for some great deals. For example, there are some transatlantic one-way business class awards that cost under 30,000 points, which is amazing.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 52,500-60,000 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Flying Club points to be worth 1.1 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Flying Club points than that.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points don’t expire. There’s no requirement to even have any account activity, as the points will never expire regardless.

While buying Virgin Atlantic points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Flying Club points. Most significantly, Virgin Atlantic is partners with major transferable points currencies, including American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou, and in all cases, points can be moved at a 1:1 ratio. There are several ways to earn these points aside from outright buying them.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is offering members an 80% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for 1.09-1.39 cents each (in USD), depending on where your account is registered.

There are plenty of circumstances where this could be a great deal. The only major consideration is that there are lots of other ways to earn Virgin Atlantic points with transferable points currencies, so some may prefer to earn rewards that way. With a specific use in mind, there could definitely be huge value in buying Flying Club points.

Do you plan on buying Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus?

#5970. Delta Air Lines Thought It Said Goodbye To Queen Of The Skies Until It Had No Choice But To Fly It Again 31 Years Later

Delta Air Lines first started operating the Boeing 747 in 1970, the same year the aircraft was introduced. The carrier grew its fleet of 747s to five aircraft, but it operated the Queen of the Skies for far less time than its rivals. Delta was optimistic about what the aircraft could bring to American aviation, but it soon found the jet too large to operate its routes efficiently.

Delta may have turned its back on the 747 in 1977, but over three decades later it would not have a choice. In 2010, the carrier merged with Northwest Airlines to create the world's largest airline at the time. Northwest was a key 747 operator, so some of the jumbos transferred into Delta's new merged fleet. It took a few years before Delta could shed all of these aircraft.

"The 747 is totally unlike any other aircraft, piston or jet. A triumph of American technology, the 747 will bring to our passengers a standard of comfort and convenience no longer limited by the size of an aircraft cabin." This is what former Delta SVP of Marketing TM Miller said of what he expected the Boeing 747-100 to bring to US aviation.

The first 747 entered Delta's fleet in September 1970. It was registered N9896 and named 'Georgia Belle.' Four more units (N9897, N9898, N9899, and N9900) arrived in November 1971. They had the serial numbers 82, 94, 155, and 159, which marked them as being within the first 200 747s built.

Delta used these aircraft to connect its major destinations in the US, such as Chicago, Detroit, Miami, New York, and San Francisco. The airline also used the jet as part of its Delta/Pan Am European interchange​​​​​. These transatlantic destinations included London and Frankfurt.

Delta's 747-100 had many unique features that it hoped would attract premium passengers.

For instance, the Delta Museum writes that the 747 "offered the world's first flying penthouse apartment located above the First Class cabin and adjacent to the First Class lounge." The unit had seats for six passengers and was staffed by a flight attendant. The jet was also the first Delta aircraft with overhead luggage bins, replacing the open racks on older aircraft. Each passenger also had access to a personal audio system with seven channels, playing a mixture of classical and pop music.

Delta acquired the 747-100 hoping it would bring unmatched size and passenger comfort to its network. Yet, the airline found that its size was actually too large for the demand available on its network. Despite the aircraft's high capacity, it routinely flew with just 100 or 200 passengers onboard when being used for domestic trunk routes.

Therefore, ticket sales could not offset the aircraft's incredibly high operating costs. Greater profitability could be gained with efficient twinjet aircraft, which serves as an interesting precursor to why quadjets are now largely obsolete. The table below shows the specifications for the 747-100, using data from Delta Museum. They give context to the aircraft's considerable size.

370 (66 first class including the penthouse and 304 in economy class)

4 x Pratt & Whitney JT9D-1 producing 164,000 lbf (730 kN)

October 25, 1970 (Atlanta-Dallas-Los Angeles)

In September 1974, Delta began to trade its 747s back to Boeing, with the final flight occurring on April 23, 1977. This left the Lockheed L-1011 as Delta's only widebody aircraft, a position it held until the first Delta Boeing 767 arrived in 1982.

These smaller widebody jets had much lower operating costs, an appropriate capacity for the level of demand domestically, and were cheaper to maintain. Although Delta has long since retired the L-1011, 57 767s remain in service according to Planespotters.net.

Captain Beverly Dickerson, who had the most flying time of any Delta pilot at the time, took the controls of Delta's last 747-100 flight. After 36 years of service, Dickerson would also retire with this journey from Atlanta to Dallas to Los Angeles. Dickerson also flew Delta's first scheduled 747 service.

The final service also included the cream of Delta's cabin crew at the time. It was staffed entirely by those who had previously worked as Passenger Service Supervisors aboard 747s. Marlene Curtiss took the PSS role for the final 747 flight. The table below shows the top ten airlines by 747-100 deliveries according to Boeing data.

Delta estimated that the aircraft flew 15,220 hours, making 13,548 takeoffs and landings in the airline's service. This aircraft was also the first Delta 747 seen in Europe as part of the Delta-Pan Am European interchange. The wife of Captain Norman Topshe, who was a retired Delta 747 captain, wrote a poem titled Adieu to the 747 in memory of the retired aircraft. It concludes:

"And so with fond memories and much appreciation, we bid you farewell - safe future destinations."

Delta thought that it had turned its back on the 747, going from strength to strength with the 767, and other widebody jets like the Airbus A310, McDonnell Douglas MD-11, and Boeing 777. However, decades later, it would have the 747 back in its fleet via a merger with Northwest Airlines.

The airlines officially completed the deal in October 2008, and integration was completed by January 2010. This created the world's largest airline at the time, operating a total of 786 aircraft and with a collective value of $17.7 billion. The merger followed hard times for both carriers. In 2005, Northwest Airlines filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, a move also completed by Delta.

Both of the carriers were members of the SkyTeam alliance, making them compatible partners. The table below shows the Northwest Airlines fleet in 2002, as published in World Traveler Magazine. This fleet would have been highly similar to the one operated during the merger. However, the merger was not a silver bullet for the airline's struggles.

The global financial crisis also created an incredibly challenging environment for the new airline. In the opening years, it was forced to cut staff and services, reduce capacity, and sell off facilities. The new airline also had to reckon with Northwest Airlines' sizable fleet, which lacked commonality and included jets that were not compatible with Delta's operations, such as the 16 747-400s.

The carrier used inherited 747-400s to power its global routes until 2017.

The newly merged airline flew 67,000 times with the 747-400 from 2009 to 2017. The peak year in terms of usage was 2013, which saw 11,300 flights and 4.3 million seats available. The aircraft operated 18 nonstop routes. Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT) was a significant destination, with the 747 helping to establish the airline's mini-hub there.

Other destinations included Ben Gurion International Airport (TLV), Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS), and Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG). The 747 managed to achieve this second lease of life because the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787 remained years away from their first deliveries.

Furthermore, while the 747 had higher fuel burn, its greater capacity meant it could outperform the Boeing 777 in some markets. Northwest Airlines' infrastructure also allowed the airline to keep using the jets. Delta gained experienced 747 crews, simulators, spare parts inventory, and maintenance personnel. Dismantling this system while the merger was ongoing would have caused more harm than good.

Delta flew its final 747 for the last time in February 2018, when flight DL9771 touched down in Marana, Arizona, for storage and cannibalization. The 213-minute journey from Arizona marked the final time in almost 50 years that Americans could buy a 747 ticket from a US airline.

CNN reported that when the 747 rolled down its last taxiway, flight attendant Stephanie Nielson said that “We’d like to welcome you to the boneyard. Now we say farewell to the queen, the last queen; it’s her last voyage, her last touchdown.” Along with the jet, senior Delta captain Paul Gallaher made his final flight.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Gallaher had flown with Northwest Airlines since 1983 and had been a 747 captain for 18 years. His final command had been the day before, flying a charter with his friend Stephen Hanlon for the Clemson Tigers football team. The pair had known and worked with each other for over 30 years.

#5969. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

#5968. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#5966. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?
