#5965. Boston-Bound British Airways 787-10 Declares Emergency Over Second Oil Leak In 10 Days

A British Airways Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner declared an emergency over the North Atlantic on Tuesday night after reporting an engine oil leak. The aircraft (registration: G-ZBLC) was operating flight BA239 from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) when it squawked 7700 more than four hours into the flight.

Despite a recommendation by the airline's operations team to divert to Iceland, the pilots managed to continue to Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), where the plane landed safely. The incident comes just ten days after the same aircraft shut down an engine over the Mediterranean and diverted to Athens. Tuesday's flight to Boston was the airframe's first flight back in service since the Athens diversion.

Flight tracking data shows that BA239 departed Heathrow just after 7:30 PM local time on Tuesday evening, and was over four hours into its roughly eight-hour journey to Boston when the pilots squawked 7700, indicating a general emergency. The Boeing 787-10 was cruising at around 33,000 feet and traveling at 378 knots when it declared the emergency.

Declared emergency after engine oil leak. Landed safely in Boston.

Air traffic control (ATC) recordings reveal that the pilots stated the problem was due to an engine oil leak. The pilots told Gander Air Traffic Control in Canada that the jet was losing oil when the engines were running at high power, and once they lowered the thrust, the oil leak stopped getting worse. The crew then descended to 28,000 feet and kept the engines at lower power for the remainder of the flight.

As reported by X account Flightdrama, ACARS messages during the emergency show that British Airways' maintenance had recommended a diversion to Keflavik (KEF) in Iceland. The messages also indicated that the same jet had previously experienced an oil leak issue, in reference to a diversion incident just ten days prior to Tuesday night's incident.

BA239 ultimately landed safely in Boston at 10:55 PM EST, around an hour after its scheduled 9:50 PM arrival. Flying lower and slower than planned — at under 400 knots, compared with a typical cruise speed close to 500 knots — added time to the journey. It remains to be seen whether authorities will open an investigation into the emergency. Simple Flying has contacted British Airways regarding this incident and will update our coverage upon response.

The aircraft involved, G-ZBLC, experienced an engine shutdown emergency on November 14, while it was operating BA105 from Heathrow to Dubai International Airport (DXB). The widebody was roughly three hours into the flight when the crew shut down the right-hand engine and diverted to Athens (ATH).

According to The Aviation Herald, a passenger on the flight reported that the pilots announced the cause of the diversion as an oil leak, although this has not been confirmed by the airline. However, ACARS messages during Tuesday night's incident cited a previous oil leak during a diversion, suggesting this did happen.

Unlike on BA105, Tuesday's pilots did not shut down an engine, instead managing the problem by reducing thrust. Tracking data shows the aircraft remained on the ground in Athens for six days, until it was repositioned back to Heathrow on November 20. It then stayed in London for another four days before re-entering service on Tuesday with the flight to Boston.

The 787 and A350 are becoming even more competitive with one another.

G-ZBLC first flew in September 2020 but was not delivered to British Airways until December 2022, after being caught up in Boeing's prolonged pause in 787 deliveries over production quality issues. It operated its first revenue flight on December 23, 2022, to Denver International Airport (DEN).

BA's 787-10s can seat up to 256 passengers across four cabins and operate long-haul routes to destinations including Boston, Newark, Seattle, Nairobi, Lagos, and Dubai. With a total of 44 Dreamliners in its fleet, the carrier is one of the few airlines globally to operate all three variants, namely the 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10.

Another of the airline's 787-10s was involved in a mishap this month after getting stuck in the mud at Heathrow ahead of a flight to Lagos. The jet was taxiing towards the runway when it failed to complete a left turn and ran onto the grass verge, with its nose landing gear sinking into the ground.

#5964. Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:

The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:

Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM

The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

Yes, but only if you choose not to travel. U.S. Department of Transportation rules require airlines to issue prompt refunds to passengers whose flight is canceled or significantly delayed. But passengers aren't eligible for a refund if they take a later flight.

Yes. DOT refund rules govern all flight disruptions, even flights canceled or delayed because of bad weather.

If the airline owes you a refund, federal rules require the carrier to refund your money within seven days if you paid by credit card, or 20 days if you paid by a different means.

It's been a chaotic couple of weeks for air travel in America, between tech outages and bad weather. Now, the holiday rush is here.

And with millions of travelers heading to airports, it's an important time to brush up on one of the most important rights that passengers have: getting a refund.

In the U.S., passengers don't have a ton of protection when it comes to delays and cancellations.

However, the federal government does have clear rules about when an airline must issue a refund.

Let's quickly walk through when you're owed a refund — and when you're not — so you can know what to ask for the next time you encounter flight trouble.

Read more: Is air travel ready for the holidays? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

For domestic flights, as well as international flights departing or arriving in the U.S., you’re covered by the rules of the U.S. Department of Transportation.

Under the DOT flight refund policy, you are entitled to a refund, no questions asked, if your flight is canceled and you ultimately choose not to travel. It doesn’t matter whether the cancellation was the airline’s fault or due to something beyond its control, like bad weather.

The policy applies to any unflown portion of your ticket.

The DOT refund rules also apply when a flight is significantly delayed or when the airline makes a significant schedule change.

Again, though, this is only if you choose not to travel.

According to federal law, a significant delay occurs when a domestic flight arrives at its destination at least three hours late, or an international flight arrives six hours late.

That also applies when the airline decides to change a flight's schedule.

Here's the big catch: You're only owed a refund if you choose not to travel, and you don't accept rebooking.

Your right to a refund is helpful if you run into a flight cancellation and delay and choose to:

The federal refund rules are less helpful if you need to fly to your destination and don't have a better backup option.

If your airline cancels your 8 a.m. flight and rebooks you on a later flight — even if it's a lot later —  your carrier would not technically owe you a refund if you agree to take that later flight.

In recent years, you may have heard about the federal government passing stricter rules when it comes to flight refunds.

That did happen, but the rules still aren't ironclad.

The actual criteria for when passengers are owed a refund didn't meaningfully change, though.

By law, airline refunds are expected "promptly" — within seven days for passengers who paid by credit card and within 20 days for those who paid by another means.

Airlines are allowed to offer passengers a voucher (or miles) instead of a refund.

However, refund-eligible passengers don’t have to accept a voucher. They can insist on simply getting their money back instead.

Know the fine print: Under the DOT's policy, if an airline wants to offer you miles when you're technically due a refund, they have to clearly disclose that.

Think carefully before accepting airline miles instead of a cash refund. You'll want to make sure you're truly getting better value. Consult TPG’s points and miles valuations to check the value of what the airline is offering in loyalty currency.

Remember: Airlines tend to devalue miles over time, so if you do accept miles, we'd suggest using them as soon as possible.

Compensation for things like meals, an unexpected hotel stay or an Uber ride in the event of a flight delay or cancellation falls under a different category than refunds.

Many airlines make guarantees about what they’ll provide in the event of a cancellation or significant delay. Those promises are laid out on the DOT’s airline customer service dashboard.

These promises are more discretionary forms of compensation. In other words, the airlines don't technically have to offer those meal vouchers or hotel bookings. Think of this as more of a goodwill gesture that the airlines have promised their customers they'll provide ... depending on the circumstances.

Also, airlines generally offer compensation only for hotel, meal and ground transportation when it's a "controllable" disruption — in other words, when it's the airline's fault.

I wouldn't count on that hotel voucher if your flight is canceled due to a winter storm or air traffic control delays.

This is where a credit card that offers travel insurance protections can be crucial (and, for me, really eliminates the financial stress of flight troubles).

Check out TPG’s guide to passenger rights for a better sense of what you might be owed.

Just prior to leaving office, the Biden administration proposed rules requiring airlines to pay passengers additional cash compensation when the carrier caused a cancellation or major delay.

However, the Trump administration opted not to move forward with that measure.

It can be challenging to keep track of airline policies, but the federal rules that govern refunds are relatively straightforward.

You are owed a refund for any unused portion of your ticket if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or has a significant schedule change (no matter the reason) and you ultimately choose not to travel with that airline. That refund should come automatically and within seven days if you paid by credit card, or 20 days if you paid using a different method.

It’s likely you are not entitled to a refund if:

Passengers who feel that an airline hasn't followed protocol or has unfairly denied a refund request can file a complaint with the DOT.

#5961. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#5960. Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card

Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

The card also has no extra cost to add authorized users, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:

Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

Southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

Preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

On your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

That said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:

The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:

I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

If you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

If you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.

#5959. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself…

Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

Getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

Ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

#5958. Giving Howard Lutnick His Due: China Is a Hard Problem

Why was Xi blocking the exported chips the Trump administration was willing to give him?

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and an Nvidia AI chip

Why wasn’t China taking the chips? The ones President Trump was willing to sell them — for a piece of the action, naturally. The ones Xi Jinping didn’t need to steal.

The question presents, for me, another valuable lesson in humility — in what Rich Lowry and I discussed on our podcast this week as the imperative of checking your premises when real-world events pose unexpected complications.

#5957. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#5956. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

#5954. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#5953. Populism Isn’t Built for Setbacks

The competitive advantage of conservatism over populism is that we are prepared for the inevitability of defeats.

President Donald Trump departs the White House, July 15, 2025, and supporters gather for a midterm campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, October 7, 2026.

NR Illustration; Jonathan Ernst, Callaghan O’Hare/Reuters

Populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising. While populist agendas can come in many different varieties, they are all propelled by a broad sense that the people — or more properly, The People — are being held back by some elite force, whether that be Big Business or an insular political establishment or something darker. If only we can overcome the enemy, we are told, we will sweep to victory on the broad, sunny uplands.

As I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared. And so it goes from there, because populism always sooner or later must decide to cling to its narratives when forced to choose between them and empirical reality:

#5952. BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On

BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:

On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:

Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed…

I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:

I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:

What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know…

It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”

What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

#5951. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#5949. How Washington Could Exploit Qatar’s LNG Shopping Spree

The U.S. may have a chance to drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.

A tanker sails past ExxonMobil and QatarEnergy’s Golden Pass LNG facility in Port Arthur, Texas, April 2, 2026.

Brett Coomer/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images

America’s leading natural gas competitor is on track to become its biggest customer. With traffic down through the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar is betting on U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG). The state’s energy company, QatarEnergy, signed two purchase agreements for American LNG in late October and is reportedly in talks with U.S. supplier Venture Global for a third. There may yet be more deals coming down the pike, including one with Houston-based NextDecade. QatarEnergy already owns 70 percent of Golden Pass LNG, a joint venture with ExxonMobil that shipped its first cargo out of Sabine Pass, Texas, in April.

Doha’s ventures are adding up. So much so that, according to an early November Financial Times report, Qatar may become “the biggest U.S. LNG buyer” by 2033. This presents the United States with opportunities to affirm market leadership and drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.

Natalie Ecanow is a research analyst for the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies. Her work focuses on the Middle East.
